Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Truthful One (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says at the beginning of Surat Ta-Ha(1):

﴿Ta-Ha. (1)﴾.

We have spoken much about the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a, the letters that occur at the openings of some surahs) at the beginnings of surahs, and there is no harm in pointing out here what has been reported about (Ta-Ha). Some hold that they are connected letters, and that it is a name of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Others hold that they are disjointed letters like (Alif-Lam-Mim) and like (Ya-Sin); they are disjointed letters, but they happen to coincide with a name, as in (Nun), which is a letter and also the name of the fish: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger... (87)﴾ (al-Anbiya') and (Qaf), which is a letter and also the name of a mountain called Mount Qaf.

So there is no objection to these letters indicating a name, and thus (Ta-Ha) is a name of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, specifically, and what follows it is:

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed. (2)﴾ (Ta-Ha).

But you notice here an anomaly: the ta and the ha were pronounced without the hamza, although they are disjointed letters like alif-lam-mim. Yet the letter was not pronounced in full, because they found the hamza burdensome and lightened it, as in dhi'b (wolf), which they say as dhib, and in bi'r (well), which they say as bir. This pronunciation supports the view that it is a name of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

We have previously clarified that the openings of surahs with disjointed letters differ from the rest of the Qur'an's verses, for all the verses of the Qur'an from its beginning to its end are built on continuity (al-wasl, connected recitation), although you may pause (waqf). Therefore all the copies of the Mushaf are built on continuity within the verses and within the surahs, so the end of a surah is recited connected to the basmala of the surah that follows it.

You say: ﴿Do you perceive of them any one or hear from them any whisper? (98)﴾ (Maryam), and (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) even at the end of the surahs of the Qur'an and its conclusion you say: ﴿Of the jinn and of mankind. (6)﴾ (al-Nas), then (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful), although it is the last word of the Qur'an, and what would come after it? But it came in continuity as an indication that the Qur'an is connected, its beginning to its end. Parts of it are not isolated from one another, so beware of neglecting it, or of thinking that you have finished it, for its end is connected to its beginning. So we read ﴿of the jinn and of mankind﴾ (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds...

So the whole Qur'an, in every sentence, every verse and every surah, is built on continuity, except that at the openings of surahs with disjointed letters, it is built on pause (Alif – Lam – Mim). This is one of the aspects of its inimitability (i'jaz), and that the Qur'an is not mechanical, but a miraculous speech from the Lord of the worlds.

Therefore, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made clear the independence of these letters in themselves, when he said: "Learn this Qur'an, for you are rewarded for its recitation, with each letter ten good deeds. I do not say that Alif-Lam-Mim is one letter, but Alif is a letter, Lam is a letter, and Mim is a letter, with each letter ten good deeds." (3)

1 Surat Ta-Ha is surah number 20 in the arrangement of the noble Mushaf. Its verses number (135), and it is a Meccan surah according to all: it was revealed before the conversion of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is surah number (44) in the order of the revelation of the Qur'an, and it was revealed after Surat Maryam and before Surat al-Waqi'a. It is a Meccan surah, but two verses are excepted from it: ﴿So bear patiently what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased. (130) And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to categories of them, the splendour of the worldly life, that We may test them therein. But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting. (131)﴾ (Ta-Ha).
Al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an (1/42) that they are both Medinan.

2 Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of (Ta-Ha) is "O man." Al-Bayhaqi reported it. It was also said by al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima said it is so in Syriac. Al-Mahdawi reported it. Al-Tabari related that it is in Nabataean "O man." Here is the view of al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4337).

3 Reported by al-Darimi in his Sunan (2/429), Fada'il al-Qur'an, chapter: on one who recites the Qur'an, from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 2:

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched.﴾

Al-shaqa' (wretchedness) is fatigue, exhaustion and toil. So Allah, glorified is He, negates for His Messenger ﷺ the fatigue caused by the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. Then, what is the counterpart? The counterpart is: "We have sent down the Qur'an upon you so that you may be happy." He is happy first because He chose you to be fit for the descent of the Qur'an upon you, and happy because you train yourself first upon the method of Allah and the doing of good, all good.

So why, then, did the word ﴿to make you wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha) come?

This is the speech of the disbelievers like Abu Jahl, Muti' ibn 'Adi, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, when they went to the Prophet ﷺ and said to him:

"You have made yourself wretched with this call (da'wa)."[1]

And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah sent me as a mercy to the worlds."[2]

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent to be happy, and his people and all people to be made happy with him, not to be wretched and to make people wretched with him. But from where did the disbelievers bring this matter of wretchedness? If the believer looks at the method of Allah with which the Qur'an was sent down, he finds that it intervenes in his desires and choices, and stands before his appetites; it commands him with what he dislikes and what burdens his self, and forbids him what he is accustomed to and loves.

So the method of Allah is against the wishes of free choice, and this tires the self and burdens it when the means is separated from its end, when one looks at the world and the obligation as separate from the Hereafter and the recompense.

As for the believer, he joins the means with the end, and toils in this world in hope of the reward in the Hereafter, so he is made happy by the method of Allah and is never made wretched by it.

Like the student who bears the hardship of study and learning, because he keeps in mind the joy of success and passing at the end of the year.

From here these disbelievers saw in the method of Allah hardship and toil, because they isolated the means from its end; therefore they felt hardship, whereas the believers felt the delight of worship and the pleasure of the obligation from Allah. This matter is what made them take gods that have no demands, no method, and no obligation, gods they worship according to their whims, and walk in their shade according to the state of their feelings.

Therefore the Qur'an made clear that they are heedless in this matter, so He said: ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha).

Or wretchedness may mean: his exposure to the stubborn leaders of Quraysh and their chieftains, who mocked him, harmed him, and set upon him their fools and boys, who insulted him and pelted him with stones, while he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made himself wretched by calling them and by eagerness for their guidance.

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, also negates wretchedness in this sense: ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha), i.e., that you should wear yourself out with them; We sent it down only so that you convey it to them.[3] This meaning recurs often in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this message﴾ (al-Kahf 6), and His saying: ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the sky, and their necks would remain humbled before it﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 4).

We have previously given an example of this, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: a man who has two slaves; he ties one of them to himself with a rope, and frees the other. When he calls them and both respond to his command, which of them is more obedient to him and more respectful of his command?

Without doubt, the free one who is at liberty, because he came by choice, whereas he was able to disobey. Likewise your Lord, blessed and exalted is He, wants you to come to Him free, by choice, a believer, while you are able not to believe.

Some people delight in criticizing Islam and accusing the Messenger ﷺ, saying: "The Messenger of Allah errs and Allah corrects him." We say: What harm is that to you? As long as his Lord is the one who corrects him, were you the ones who corrected the Messenger of Allah? Then who told you of the Messenger of Allah's error? Is it not he who told you? Is this not from the strength of his trustworthiness in conveying, which you ought to praise him for?

So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not disdain that his Lord should educate him; therefore he says: "I am only a human being; a matter is presented to me — meaning from the Truth — so I say: I am not like any one of you; and it is taken from me, so I say: I am only a human like you."

These people have contrived much regarding the story of Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was occupied with the great men of Quraysh. One who reflects on this story finds that Ibn Umm Maktum was a believing man who came to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about something; so speaking with him was easy and simple, whereas those were the heads of disbelief and the great men of the people, and they had, besides that, obstinate enmity against Islam. The Prophet ﷺ was eager for their guidance and wore himself out in arguing with them, hoping that Allah would guide through them those beneath them.

So the Prophet ﷺ in this situation chose for himself the harder course, and his Lord reproved him for that; it is a reproof for his benefit, to his advantage, not against him.[4]

[1] Muqatil said: Abu Jahl and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are indeed wretched in abandoning our religion," because of what they saw of his long worship and diligence; so Allah sent down this verse: ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha). (Mentioned by al-Wahidi al-Nisaburi in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 174.)

[2] Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (5/257) from the hadith of Abu Umama, may Allah be pleased with him, and its completion: "Indeed Allah sent me as a mercy and guidance to the worlds, and commanded me to obliterate the flutes, the strings, the wind instruments, and the idols that were worshipped in the Jahiliyya."

[3] Al-Tirmidhi recorded in his Sunan (3318) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in a long hadith, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah sent me only as a conveyer, and did not send me as one who causes hardship." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."

[4] On this the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him. As for one who thinks himself self-sufficient, to him you attend. And it is not upon you that he should not purify himself. But as for one who comes to you striving, and he fears [Allah], from him you are distracted. No! Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it﴾ (Abasa).

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Only as a reminder to those who fear﴾ (3).

That is: We did not send the Qur'an down upon you so that you would be distressed. Rather, We sent it down as a reminder (tadhkirah), that is, as admonition (tadhkir), for those who fear (yakhsha). Khashyah (reverent fear) is fear accompanied by awe (mahabah), because fear may exist without awe, whereas fear of Allah is both fear and awe together.

Tanzilan (تنزيلا): a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "We sent it down in stages (tanzilan)." Regarding the descent of the Qur'an, the following forms occur: "anzalnahu" (We sent it down), "nazzalnahu" (We sent it down gradually), and "nazala" (it descended). The Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree. And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by permission of their Lord, with every matter.﴾ (al-Qadr).

The Qur'an went through several stages of descent. It was first in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), then God willed that the Qur'an should begin its task in existence, so He sent it down from the Preserved Tablet, all at once, to the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya). Then it descended to the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) piece by piece, according to events, from the lowest heaven, and the one who brought it down was Gabriel: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ (al-Shu'ara').

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ (Ta-Ha, 4).

He specified the heavens and the earth because they are among the greatest of God's creations. God prepared them to receive mankind. Man arrived in a universe already prepared and ready to receive him, so at the moment he sees this universe prepared for his service, with its earth and its sky, and with no power to direct any part of it, it is incumbent upon him to use his intellect and to infer from them the Originator, glory be to Him.

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is saying to you: if the Creator, glorified is He, has prepared for you the universe with that which sustains your material life, would He leave your spiritual life without provision?

The Creator, mighty and majestic is He, created this universe with a just, wise, and self-sustaining design that provides His vicegerent on earth with the preservation of his life, and gives him everything he needs in precise measure. Preserving life requires food, drink, and air, and God has given these to man with consummate wisdom.

Man needs food, and he can endure without eating for a month. He needs water, but he cannot endure without it for more than ten days. He needs air, and he cannot endure without it for even a moment that lasts several breaths.

Therefore, it is of God's mercy toward His servants that food is owned by some people, so you have a long time to devise means of earning it, whereas few own water. As for air, which you cannot endure without, it is of God's wisdom that no one owns it; otherwise, if anyone withheld air from you, you would die before he was satisfied with you.

Thus it is of God's wisdom that He created your body to receive the constituents of sustaining life for a period of time wide enough for ingenuity and for the compassion of others. When you eat, the body takes what it needs in proportion to the energy expended, and what overflows is stored in your body as fat, which nourishes the body when food is unavailable.

And among the wonders of God's power is that this fatty substance transforms spontaneously into any other substance the body needs: if it needs iron, it transforms chemically into iron, and if it needs arsenic, it transforms chemically into arsenic, though in reality it is one substance. Who but Him, exalted is He, can perform this process?

After providing you with what sustains your life, food, drink, and air, He gave you what perpetuates your kind through marriage and procreation.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the high heavens﴾ (Ta-Ha, 4): al-ula is the plural of ulya, just as we say in the plural of kubra (greatest): kubar, as in ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (al-kubar)﴾ (al-Muddaththir, 35).

Thus the elevated constitution of God's vicegerent on earth is completed. Just as He provided him with what sustains his life and his kind through the creation of the heavens and the earth, He provided him with what sustains his spirit through the descent of the Qur'an, which guards our movements from the savagery of desires. The One who sent down the Qur'an is the One who created the earth and the high heavens.

The prominent attribute of this elevated constitution of man is the attribute of al-Rahmaniyya (the Most Merciful); therefore after it He said: ﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾ (Ta-Ha, 5).

The preceding verse gave us one aspect of kindness and mercy, and this one gives us an aspect of dominance and supremacy. The istiwa' (rising over, settling) of the Most Merciful, blessed and exalted, upon the Throne is to be understood within the framework of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ (al-Shura: 11). We have already spoken about the attributes shared between the Truth, glory be to Him, and His creation: you have hearing and sight, and God has hearing and sight, but beware of thinking that God's hearing is like your hearing, or that His sight is like your sight.

Likewise with the matter of istiwa' upon the Throne: the Truth, glory be to Him, has an istiwa' upon His Throne, but it is not like your istiwa' upon the chair, for example.(1)

In the custom of the Arabs, the 'arsh (Throne) is the couch of the king. Does a king sit upon his couch to attend to the affairs of his kingdom and manage its concerns except after his rule has been firmly established?

Likewise the Creator, majestic and exalted, created the universe with its earth and its heavens, and created the creatures, and sent down the Qur'an to organize their lives. And after His rule was firmly established, He did not leave the universe to operate mechanically in this manner, nor did He withdraw from His universe and His creatures, because they are in need of His qayyumiyyah (self-subsisting sustaining power, exalted be He) over His creation.

Did not the Truth, glory be to Him, say in the hadith qudsi: (O My servants, sleep to your hearts' content, for I am al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting), who does not sleep.)(2)

Thus God's universe is not a machine that operates of its own accord; rather He is standing in His qayyumiyyah over it and does not depart from it. Therefore the miracles that break the laws of the universe were a proof of this qayyumiyyah.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4341): (What Shaykh Abu al-Hasan and others adopted is that He is established upon His Throne without limit and without modality, just as the settling of created beings is. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the creation of what was and what will be until the Day of Resurrection and after the Resurrection.) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/142): (The safest path in this is the method of the Salaf: letting pass what has come concerning it in the Book and the Sunnah without modality (takyif), distortion (tahrif), likening (tashbih), negation (ta'til), or representation (tamthil).)

2 Ibn Kathir cited in his tafsir (1/309) from Ibn 'Abbas that the Children of Israel said: "O Musa, does your Lord sleep?" He said: "Fear God." Then his Lord, mighty and majestic, called to him: "O Musa, they have asked you whether your Lord sleeps. Take two glass vessels in your hands and stand up tonight." Musa did so. When a third of the night had passed, he dozed and fell onto his knees, then recovered and steadied them; until at the end of the night he dozed, and the two vessels fell and broke. He said: "O Musa, if I were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would fall and perish just as the two vessels in your hands perished."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil (6)﴾.

Al-Haqq (the Truth), blessed and exalted is He, bestows favour by what He owns in the heavens, on the earth, and beneath the soil; and Allah, exalted is He, mentions only the ownership of a precious thing from which one benefits.

It is as if He, glorified is He, draws the attention of His creatures to what exists in the universe of the foundations of their material life, so that they may search for them and derive what He has stored up for them of secrets and wealth in the heavens and the earth. One who looks into the civilisations of nations finds that they came either from the excavations of the earth or from the secrets of outer space in the age of space.

Had the Muslims understood this verse from the time it was revealed, they would have known that in the earth, and beneath the soil, which is: (the dust), there are treasures and wealth that they did not know until the modern era, after discoveries and excavations; so we found petroleum, minerals and precious stones, all buried beneath the soil, awaiting one who will dig for them and benefit from them.

The scholars have explained that these riches are distributed across God's earth evenly, such that if equal sections were taken from different lands you would find the riches in them equal: this one has water, this one has crops, this one has minerals, this one has petroleum, and so on. They are like a watermelon when you divide it into equal pieces from the surface to the centre.

Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure (21)﴾ (al-Hijr).

So then: goodness exists, awaiting the decree so that it may appear to us and we may benefit from it.

Then He, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾

The Truth, glory be to Him, when He asks His Messenger to remember Him, wants him to remember Him in a manner tied to his intention, not merely to clear himself of blame. So the matter is not one of remembrance aloud.

If God says to His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace: "I shall guard your secret as I guard your openness, and loud speech is to Me like secret speech, indeed more hidden than secret speech," and he, may God bless him and grant him peace, is entrusted with the message, then He also says to his community: "Beware lest you say words whose outward form is mercy while your intention is settled upon something else, for God knows what is spoken aloud just as He knows the secret, and what is more hidden than the secret."

We have spoken of loud speech, which is that you let someone who wishes to hear, hear. The secret is that you single out one person and place in his ear words you do not want to spread among people, whispering to him that you trust him with this speech. You feel at ease in yourself when you confide your secret to someone you trust, and feel safe that he will not broadcast it. In the life of each of us there are matters that constrict the soul, so you must find release for yourself, as the poet said:

"There must be a complaint to one of noble character,
who will console you, or soothe you, or grieve with you."

So you are, then, in need of one who will listen to you in order to relieve you and release you, and who will not expose you with what you confided to him.

The meaning of ﴿and what is yet more hidden﴾ (Ta-Ha 7): that is, more hidden than the secret. If your secret has come out of your mouth into the ear of your listener, there is something more hidden than the secret, namely what you have kept to yourself and not uttered to anyone.

Therefore He, exalted, says: ﴿And keep your word secret or speak it aloud, indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ (al-Mulk 13): that is, its hidden contents before they become speech.

He also says: ﴿And We know what his soul whispers to him...﴾ (Qaf 16): so the whispering of the soul and what is within the breasts is the most hidden beyond the secret. Thus we have loud speech, secret speech, and what is more hidden than the secret. But some of the knowers say: there is in God's knowledge something more hidden than the most hidden. What is it? He says: He, exalted, knows what will be in the soul before it comes to be.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 8:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, brought the word with which all the messengers were sent: ﴿Allah! There is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.(8)﴾.

This word ("There is no god but Him") is the summit of belief, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said of it: "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: There is no god but Allah."(1)

Since there is no god but Allah, He is the One entrusted with you. There is no other god to whom one may refer or appeal. So work for His countenance and He will suffice you in every direction, relieve your soul of being pulled by many different and conflicting powers, and make you independent of every other need.

When a Bedouin (a‘rabi) entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was speaking with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), he could not understand anything of what the two were saying. So he said: "O Messenger of Allah, I do not know how to murmur as you murmur, nor as Abu Bakr murmurs. I only know: There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Around it we murmur, O brother of the Arabs."(2)

So this is the foundation and the center around which Islam revolves.

The word (Allah) is the proper name denoting the Necessarily Existent, possessing all the attributes of perfection: Allah the Existing, Allah the Capable, Allah the Knowing, Allah the Living, Allah the Giver of Life, Allah the Harmful. All these are attributes of Him, glory be to Him. But these attributes, when they reached the limit of perfection in Him, the Exalted, became like a proper name, such that when the Creator (al-Khaliq) is mentioned it refers only to Him, and the Provider (al-Razzaq) refers only to Him.

Creatures may share some attributes with the Creator, as in His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, then provide for them...(8)﴾ (al-Nisa').

Man too provides, but his provision is from within the provision of Allah; He is the Supreme Provider, and from His sea everyone draws.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.(14)﴾ (al-Mu'minun), and He said: ﴿And you invent a falsehood.....(17)﴾ (al-'Ankabut).

Does this mean there are creators other than Him, glory be to Him? The meaning of creating is bringing into existence from non-existence. Whoever brought sand and made from it a cup is a creator of the cup, for you brought something into existence from non-existence, and Allah brought something into existence from non-existence; but you produced from a thing existing by Allah's creation before you existed. Therefore He is "the best of creators," and yet your Lord did not withhold from you by granting you the title of creator, and this obliges you to be fair to Him and say: ﴿the best of creators(14)﴾ (al-Mu'minun).

Also, when Allah, the Exalted, honors your bringing into existence of something non-existent and names you a creator, and does not withhold from you by granting you one of His attributes, He is informing you that He is the best of creators, because you bring into existence something non-existent which remains in the state you brought it and stays fixed in that condition. But the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, brings into existence something non-existent, grants it life, makes it meet its like, and it procreates. Can a man who made a cup make from it a male and a female that produce cups for us? And does the small cup grow, or feel pain if it is broken, for example?

Thus, the Creator, glory be to Him, is the best of creators, and likewise He is the best of providers, the best of inheritors, and the best of planners.

As for His saying: ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names(8)﴾ (Ta-Ha): al-Husna is the superlative feminine form, like kubra, corresponding to (ahsan) for the masculine. Therefore there are beautiful names (hasana), which are the names of creatures, but the names of Allah are "most beautiful" (husna), because they have reached the summit of perfection, and because the names and attributes that apply to them exist in the Supreme Creator, glory be to Him. So when you say of the names of Allah (al-Razzaq), it is the most beautiful attribute (al-husna), not merely beautiful (al-hasana).

For this reason, when a man named Sa'd wanted to consult his father about the proposal for his daughter, Husna, to whom two men had proposed, Hasan and Ahsan, his father said to him: "Then choose Husna, O Sa'd, for the Ahsan."

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna) and more.(26)﴾ (Yunus). He did not say "hasana," because they did good and so deserved the best (husna) and more.

The names of Allah, the Exalted, are in reality attributes, but when they were applied to the Truth, blessed and exalted, they became names. You may name a black girl "Qamar" (Moon) or name a dwarf "al-Tawil" (the Tall), because when a name is used as a proper noun for another, it is detached from its original meaning and remains only a proper name. But the names of Allah remained with their original meanings even after they became proper names for Allah, the Exalted. Therefore they are "most beautiful names."

After the Truth, blessed and exalted, spoke of the Seal of the Messengers, bearer of the final method (there is no prophet after him and no method after his method), He, glory be to Him, wished to console him with a consolation that shows his position in the procession of the messages, and to give him an example of those messengers before him, and how every messenger toiled in proportion to his message. If earlier messages were limited in time and limited in place, and their bearers nevertheless toiled for them, then what of a messenger who came for all time and all place? He will inevitably face hardships like all of these.

Therefore, O Muhammad, prepare yourself to meet hardships and difficulties proportionate to your greatness in the message, your being the Seal of the Prophets, and the extension of your message through time until the Hour arrives, and through space as far as the earth extends.

For this reason, the Truth, blessed and exalted, chose for His Messenger (ﷺ) a prophet of the steadfast (ulu al-'azm), because he came to the Children of Israel and came to Pharaoh. The Children of Israel were a materialistic people, and Pharaoh claimed divinity. He chose Moses (peace be upon him) to recount his story to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and console him regarding the hardships of the call, as He said: ﴿And all that We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We strengthen your heart; and in this has come to you the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.(120)﴾ (Hud).

And He said: ﴿Say: I am not an innovation among the messengers.....(9)﴾ (al-Ahqaf).

So you, O Muhammad, are like other messengers: they found hardship in proportion to their messages, and you too will find hardship in proportion to your message. We give an example of this: a student who is satisfied with the preparatory stage, another with secondary school or university, and another who strives for a doctorate. There is no doubt that each of them exerts effort in proportion to his task. Therefore He says: ﴿And has there reached you the story(4) of Moses?(9)﴾.

1 Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3585) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "The best supplication is on the Day of 'Arafah..." the hadith in full. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This hadith is gharib from this route."
2 Ahmad related it in his Musnad (3/474), Ibn Majah in his Sunan (3847), and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (792), from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to a man: "How do you say in the prayer?" He said: "I recite the tashahhud, then I say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and seek refuge with You from the Fire, but as for me, I do not know how to murmur as you murmur, nor as Mu'adh murmurs." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Around it we murmur."
3 That is: I am not strange, nor wondrous, nor without a prior pattern; I am like the earlier messengers. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/57).
4 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4343): "The scholars of meanings said: it is an interrogative which affirms and asserts, its meaning being: has it not reached you? It was also said: its meaning is: it has reached you. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas."

When the interrogative comes from Allah, the Exalted, know that it is an interrogative not in its literal sense; it is not intended here to seek understanding, for the reports of Muhammad come to him from his Lord, glory be to Him, so how would He ask him? What is intended by the interrogative here is to create eagerness for what is about to come, just as you say to your companion: "Has the news of what happened yesterday reached you?" so that he becomes eager to hear what happened.

Al-hadith, that is, the report about him, whether it is by revelation or by other than revelation, as if I were to relate to him the story of Musa (peace be upon him)... So has this story reached you?

Listen to it now from me: ﴿When he saw a fire, and said to his family, "Wait here, for I have perceived a fire; perhaps I may bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance."﴾ (20:10)

1 Ibn 'Abbas and others said: this was when he had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, returning from Madyan heading for Egypt, and he had lost his way. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa asked Shu'ayb for permission to return to his mother, and he granted it; so he set out with his family and his flock. A son was born to him on the way, on a cold, snowy winter night, and he had strayed from the road and his flock had scattered. Musa struck the flint, but the tinder yielded him nothing, when he caught sight of a fire from afar on the left side of the road. Related by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4343).

2 Al-qabas: a flame of fire (Lisan al-'Arab, root q-b-s).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 10:

We notice here that the context does not recount the story of Musa from its beginning, when Allah said: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa, "Suckle him..."﴾ (al-Qasas 28:7), and then his leaving the city in fear and his going to Shu'ayb, and so on. Rather, it aims directly at the essence of the matter, which is the message.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you from it a burning brand or find at the fire some guidance﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10). "Ananist" (I perceived) means: I saw, and I felt something by which one feels companionship, joy, and reassurance. Its opposite is "tawajjasa" (he sensed), which refers to a harm one fears, as in His saying: ﴿So Musa sensed within himself a fear﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:67).

"La'alli" (perhaps) expresses hope that I will find in it the "qabas" (a live coal/brand), which is a flame taken from a fire when the fire is found and has a blaze; one takes from it a burning stick like a candle.

In another context He said "jadhwa" (a firebrand), which is fire when its flame has died down and embers remain from which a fire can be kindled. In another place He said: ﴿I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves﴾ (al-Naml 27:7).

All of these are multiple depictions and states of the fire, and there is no contradiction in them, as some like to claim. When Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Perhaps I can bring you...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10), he hoped to find a qabas, but he did not know the state of the fire when he reached it: would it be a qabas or a jadhwa?

Musa, peace be upon him, sought the qabas for his family because they were in a very cold, rainy night, strangers who knew nothing of the place. It was not a known path to them, so they would walk without knowing their direction. So what would Musa, peace be upon him, do, with his wife, his young son, and his servant?

They were in dire need of fire, either for warmth in this bitter weather or to seek guidance on the way. Therefore he said: ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10), meaning a guide who would show us the way.

In another place he said: ﴿Perhaps I can bring you from it some news﴾ (al-Qasas 28:29). Therefore, when Musa, peace be upon him, saw the fire, he hurried to it after reassuring his family: ﴿Stay here, indeed I have perceived a fire...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10).

This matter in the story of Musa was a cause of doubt for the enemies of Islam, who found different contexts for one story. Once He says: ﴿Stay here, indeed I have perceived a fire, perhaps I can bring...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10), and in another place He says: ﴿Perhaps I can bring you from it some news...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:29).

Once He says "qabas," and another time "bi-shihabin qabas," and once "bi-jadhwa," and once He says: ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10), and once He says: ﴿Perhaps I can bring you from it some news...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:29).

Whoever reflects on the situation that Musa, his wife, his young son, and his servant were now in, in this desolate place where the weather had grown dark over them, will find the difference in context here natural. Each of them receives the news from Musa in a particular way. When he saw the fire and informed them of it, he wanted to reassure them, so he said: ﴿I will bring you...﴾ (al-Naml 27:7). When he saw them clinging to him, saying, "Do not leave us in this place," he said: ﴿Stay...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10). Perhaps he said this to his wife and son, and said that to his servant. They must have responded to him, so the words varied around a single situation.

Likewise, in His saying "qabas or jadhwa": when he said, ﴿Perhaps I can bring you...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:10), he hoped to find a qabas there, but perhaps he would go and find a jadhwa. At another time he spoke with certainty, saying: ﴿I will bring you...﴾ (al-Naml 27:7).

So these are different snapshots that form the fabric of the complete story, and the words multiplied because the situation was open to response and does not end with a single word.

1 That is in His saying: ﴿Perhaps I can bring you from it some news or a firebrand from the fire so that you may warm yourselves﴾ (al-Qasas 28:29).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 11:

Then the Truthful Lord, glory be to Him, says: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "O Moses!"﴾ (11).

It is said: when Moses (peace be upon him) came to it, he found a light shining in a tree. But the greenness of the tree did not affect the light so as to dazzle it, nor did the light overpower the greenness of the tree so as to deprive it of its greenness. So this is a wondrous matter that none can bring about except Allah.

This fire was thus the first act of reassurance (iyna's) for Moses in this desolate place. It is as if the wondrous sight he saw was a divine preparation for Moses, so that he might receive from his Lord. The matter, then, is not merely a natural scene.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿he was called, "O Moses..."﴾ (11) (Ta-Ha): that is, in this state of astonishment, ﴿he was called﴾ (11) (Ta-Ha). The One who calls him knows him perfectly; therefore He called him by his name: ﴿"O Moses..."﴾ (11) (Ta-Ha). And since the matter is such, the hope of good in it is present, and Moses began to feel at ease with the source of the call and to be comforted by it, and he sought the source of this voice, not knowing whence it came; therefore he regarded it as a wondrous matter, like the sight of the tree from which the light emanated.

Thus, when his Lord spoke to him, "Indeed, I am your Lord" (Qur'an 20:12), He removed from his soul the wonder and astonishment at what he had seen and heard, and he knew that it was from Allah the Exalted; so he became reassured and rejoiced that he would see other wonders.

We note in His saying, "Indeed, I am your Lord" (Qur'an 20:12), that when Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, speaks of His own Essence, He speaks in the singular pronoun, "Indeed, I am your Lord" (Qur'an 20:12), and when He speaks of His act, He speaks in the plural form, as in His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: "Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree" (Qur'an 97:1), "Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder" (Qur'an 15:9), and "Indeed, We will inherit the earth and whoever is upon it" (Qur'an 19:40).

So why does He speak of the act in the plural form, while He calls us to affirm His oneness and not associate anything with Him? They said: Speaking of His Essence, may He be exalted, must involve affirming His oneness, as in: "Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance" (Qur'an 20:14).

However, in the act He speaks in the plural form, because the act requires many attributes and various capacities: it requires a will that intends it, power to execute it, capacities, knowledge and wisdom.

Therefore: all the attributes of the Truth converge in the act; for this reason the discourse about it came in the plural form. They say that the "nun" in His saying, "We sent down the Reminder" (Qur'an 15:9) and "We will inherit the earth" (Qur'an 19:40) is the nun of majesty (nun al-ta'zim).

The address to Musa came with the term of lordship: "Indeed, I am your Lord" (Qur'an 20:12), to give Musa comfort, because lordship (rububiyyah) is a bestowal. So His address "your Lord" means the One who takes charge of your care and upbringing, who created you from nothing and sustained you from nothing, and He did not say "Indeed, I am Allah," because divinity (uluhiyyah) demands obligation, worship, and restriction of movement with "do this" and "do not do that."

And His saying, "Indeed, I am your Lord" (Qur'an 20:12) means: your Lord specifically, not the absolute Lord; because the messengers differ from all creation, so they have a specific upbringing, as He said: "And that you may be raised under My eye" (Qur'an 20:39) and He said: "And I have chosen you for Myself" (Qur'an 20:41).

Therefore: the Truth, blessed and exalted, raises the messengers with an upbringing suited to the task they will perform.

And His saying, "So take off your sandals" (Qur'an 20:12): this is the first command. Removing the sandals is for humility and to show reverence, and because the place is sacred. The reason is: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa" (Qur'an 20:12). So: take off your sandals so that your body is not separated from the soil of this sacred, pure place, and do not let your sandals come between you and direct contact with the particles of this earth.

Among this is what we see in the city of the Messenger of Allah, where people walk barefoot, and one of them says: "Perhaps my foot will touch the place where the foot of His Messenger (ﷺ) stepped."

His saying "Tuwa" (Qur'an 20:12) is the name of the valley, and this is a general statement whose specification came in another place, when He, glorified, said: "So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree..." (Qur'an 28:30).

Some see in the verse a repetition. The verse is not so; rather, it is the establishment of a new statement that clarifies and specifies where the sacred valley Tuwa is. If you say: "Where is Tuwa?" he tells you: "In the right-hand valley." But the right-hand valley itself is long, so where in it is this place? He tells you: "At the blessed spot of the tree."

Therefore: the second verse specifies the place for you, just as you say: "I live in such-and-such quarter, on such-and-such street, at such-and-such number."

1 That is: I taught you, raised you, and bestowed favors upon you so that you would be a creation of Mine who serves Me and carries out the message I charge you with and have chosen you for. (al-Qamus al-Qawim (1/384)).

2 Said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others. al-Dahhak said: it is a deep, circular valley like a tawa (basin). al-Hasan said: blessing and sanctification were repeated in it twice. al-Mahdawi reported from Ibn Abbas that it was said to him that (Tuwa) is because Musa traversed it (tawahu) at night, when he passed by it and ascended to the upper part of the valley. So it is as if He said: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley" that you traversed (tuwiya), meaning you crossed it by your journey. (Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 6/4347). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/144): "The first is more correct, like His saying: 'When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa' (79:16)."

3 Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/388): "This is among what guides to the fact that Musa headed toward the fire in the direction of the qibla, with the western mountain on his right, and he saw the fire blazing in a green tree at the foot of the mountain facing the valley, so he stood bewildered at its matter."

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.﴾ (20:13)

Meaning: even if you were a lord to yourself and a lord to the disbelievers, I will add a special distinction for you. ﴿And I have chosen you﴾ (20:13), that is, for the message, and God knows best where He places His message.

Therefore the Qur'an was not revealed to our master Muhammad (ﷺ) without objection. The Meccan disbelievers raised no objection to the Qur'an, and they found no fault in what it calls to of noble morals and lofty examples. They found no flaw in its style, though they were a people who had grown accustomed to fine expression and whose ears were enamoured of eloquent speech. So they turned their criticism toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ (43:31).

Thus their entire objection was that the Qur'an should descend upon Muhammad specifically. The Qur'an therefore answered them, exposing their foolishness on this matter, saying: ﴿Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ (43:32). How could they, when We have apportioned among them their livelihood in this worldly life: ﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ (43:32).

Yet they want to apportion the mercy of God, saying: "This one is revealed upon this one, and that one upon that one?"

Then the Exalted says: ﴿so listen to what is revealed﴾ (20:13). The root s-m-' gives: sami'a (he heard), istama'a (he listened attentively), and tasam-ma'a (he made himself hear). When we say sami'a, it means by chance, as when you walk along the road and hear much speech, some of which concerns you and some of which does not. The ear has no covering that blocks hearing, as the eyelid does for the eye, for example when you see a sight you dislike.

So you hear everything that reaches your ear, and you have no choice in it.

But istama'a (listen) means to take pains to hear, and the speaker is free to speak or not to speak.

And tasammu'a means to exert great effort in order to hear.

Therefore, when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that the trial of singing would spread, and devices that would propagate this trial would multiply, pouring it into every ear against its will, he said: "Whoever listens to a qaynah, molten lead will be poured into his ears." (1)

That is, one who makes an effort to hear it and deliberately directs the radio or television toward this singing. He did not say sami'a, because otherwise everyone would be struck by this evil against his will.

Here the Exalted said ﴿fa-istami' (so listen)﴾ and did not say tasam-ma', because one does not propose to God that He speak. The meaning of istama'a is: mobilize all your limbs and prepare all your senses to hear. If the ear is for hearing, there are other senses that can distract you from attention: the eye sees, the nose smells, and the tongue speaks.

So you must mobilize all the senses in order to hear, and summon your heart to understand what you hear and carry out what is required of you. Therefore, when you address your companion and find him preoccupied with something else, you say: "It is as if you are not with us." Why? Because one of his limbs has wandered off and so has distracted him from listening.(2)

And His saying ﴿lima yuha (what is revealed)﴾ (20:13). Revelation in general is informing in concealment, from one to another, in something, whether good or evil. But shar'i revelation is information from God to a messenger He has sent, with a way of life that is good for His servants. If revelation was from God to the mother of Moses, for example, or to the disciples (al-hawariyyun), this is not shar'i revelation. Thus it is defined: from one to another, in something.

But how does revelation descend from God upon the Messenger? How does divinity in its exaltedness meet humanity in its lowliness? Therefore there must be an intermediary, and so the Exalted said: ﴿God chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind...﴾ (22:75).

The one chosen from the angels receives from God and gives to the one chosen from humankind, because the higher cannot meet the lower directly: ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or He sends a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills...﴾ (42:51).

So the human disposition and nature do not qualify him for this encounter. How could they, when the Truth, glorified and exalted, manifested Himself to the mountain and made it crumble? And from His greatness, glorified is He, we do not see Him, nor speak with Him directly, nor perceive Him by any of our senses. Had the God been perceptible by any sense, He would not deserve to be God.

And how could the Truth, blessed and exalted, be perceived by what He created and fashioned, which cannot be perceived, such as the soul, for example? We do not know its essence, nor where it is, nor do we perceive it by any of our senses. If the created soul we cannot grasp, how shall we grasp its Creator?

The truth that people claim and cling to, and each boasts that he speaks the word of truth, and likewise justice and other meanings: can you perceive them, do you know a form for them? How then do you hope to perceive the Mighty and Majestic Creator?

Therefore, from His greatness, glorified is He, He cannot be grasped by the senses, and He does not meet creation in direct encounter. The one chosen from the angels takes from God and gives to the one chosen from creation, and then the one chosen from creation gives to creation. Yet the Prophet (ﷺ) would strain, and his brow would drip with sweat at the beginning of revelation.

For this reason, God willed to withhold revelation from His Messenger for a period, so that he might rest from direct contact with the angel. With the cessation of revelation, the sweetness of what had been revealed to the Messenger of God remained, and he longed for revelation anew, so the hardship he met in the way became easier to bear, for the heart's preoccupation with a thing makes one forget its burdens.

It is also reported that when revelation descended upon him, he (ﷺ) would hear around him a humming like the humming of bees (3), and if it happened that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) placed his foot upon one of his companions while revelation descended on him, the companion would feel it as if it were a mountain; and if revelation came while he was on a mount, the mount would kneel and groan under its weight (4).

We have illustrated the intermediary between the divine nature and the human nature by electric current: when we connect it to a small lamp that cannot bear the force of the current, they place a device that regulates the current and gives the lamp according to its need, lest it burn out.

(1) The Qaynah is the female slave who sings; she is so called from adornment (tazayyun), since she adorns herself. Abu Mansur said: a singing girl is called qaynah when singing is her profession, and that is the work of slave women, not free women. (Lisan al-'Arab, root q-y-n).

(2) Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the beginning of knowledge is listening, then understanding, then memorizing, then acting, then spreading it. When the servant listens to the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet with a sincere intention, in accordance with what God loves, God makes him understand as He loves, and places light in his heart. Related by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4348).

(3) From 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), who said: "When revelation descended upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), there was heard near his face a humming like the humming of bees." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (1/34), and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (2/392), who said: "a sound hadith by its chain, though they did not record it."

(4) From Asma' bint Yazid, who said: "I was holding the reins of al-'Adba', the she-camel of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when the whole of al-Ma'ida descended upon him, and she nearly broke the camel's shoulder from its weight." Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir for surah al-Ma'ida (2/2), attributed by him to Imam Ahmad.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ (14).

In the verse before the previous one, His Lord addressed him: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾ (12) (Ta-Ha), to reassure him and comfort him, that He is the Nurturer, the Compassionate, who gives even to the disbeliever who disobeys Him. But here He addresses him with: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha), meaning: the Possessor of obligations, the Deity obeyed in commands and prohibitions, and the first and foremost of these obligations, and the wellspring from which all faithful conduct proceeds:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha):

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said of it: "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: there is no deity but Allah."¹

And since there is no deity but Him, it is not proper for us to receive commands and prohibitions except from Him, nor to rely except upon Him, nor to let anything other than Him occupy our hearts. He, glorified is He, wants us to be trustees: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾ (58) (al-Furqan).

So the wise, discerning adviser does not rely on anyone other than Allah, for you may rely on someone other than Him, then in the morning you find he is not there. The poet spoke truly when he said:

Make your might rest in your Lord,
which is steadfast and enduring.

And if you take pride in one who dies,
then your pride is dead.

So the Truth, glorified is He, in His saying: ﴿There is no deity except Me﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha), is as if saying to Moses: Do not fear; you will not receive orders from anyone other than Me. As He, glorified is He, said in another verse: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other deities, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ (42) (al-Isra').

That is: those who claim divinity would have gone to Allah, either contending with Him or seeking His favor, and none of this happened.

It is a condition of the one who gives commands, legislates and enacts laws that he gain nothing from any of that, and that his commands and prohibitions serve the interest of those commanded. Hence God's law differs from human law, which is entered by desire and mixed with interests and aims. For example, if the legislator and lawmaker is from the workers, he sides with them and raises them above the capitalists; and if he is from those, he raises them above the workers.

Likewise, nothing should escape him that could be corrected later. These conditions exist only in divine legislation. For Him, glorified is He, are the attributes of perfection before He created creation.

Therefore He said after it: ﴿so worship Me﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha), by obeying My commands and avoiding My prohibitions, for I have no desire in what I command you; it is only your benefit and your well-being.

As for the meaning of worship ('ibadah): people think it is prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage, but worship has a far broader meaning than that. Every movement in life that leads to worship is worship, as we say in the principle: whatever the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory.

For example, prayer is not complete without covering the nakedness. Consider this piece of cloth with which you cover your nakedness: how many hands have contributed to it from when it was a seed in the earth until it became a fine cloth covering your nakedness? Each one of these was in worship while performing his task in this matter.

Likewise the loaf of bread you eat, the tap from which you perform ablution: how many hands, workers, factories, scientists and capabilities have been mobilized to serve you, so that you may carry out your movement in life?

Therefore, when the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, speaks to us about the Friday prayer, He says: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade. That is better for you, if you only knew. And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah﴾ (9-10) (al-Jumu'ah).

Thus He brought us out of work into prayer, and after prayer He commanded us to work, to strive, to disperse in the land and to seek from the bounty of Allah. So disobeying the command in: ﴿hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade﴾ (9) (al-Jumu'ah) is like disobeying the command in: ﴿disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah﴾ (10) (al-Jumu'ah).

Trade is singled out here because the seller is keener to sell than the buyer is to buy, and it may be in the buyer's interest not to buy.

Thus Islam does not know idleness, nor does it accept sloth and sitting around; whoever wants stillness does not benefit from the movement of one who moves.

When our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) saw a man who stayed in the mosque and never left it, he asked: "Who spends on him?" They said: "His brother." He said: "His brother is more devoted to worship than he is." Why? Because he contributes to the movement of life and widens the benefit for people.

So every beneficial work is worship, provided the intention is present. The disbeliever works with the intention of providing for himself; if the believer does the same, what is the difference between them? The believer works, yes, to sustain himself, and also to make the sustenance and life's movement easier for his brothers. For example, if a taxi driver works until he earns an amount sufficient for him, then goes home and parks his car, who will take the sick man who needs to be driven to the doctor? And if the seller earns his livelihood then closes his shop, who will sell to the people?

So: work for yourself, but keep in mind also the interest and needs of others. If you do this, you are in worship, working according to your capacity, not according to your need; then you take your need from the product of your effort, and the rest returns to people, either as charity or for a price. It is enough for you that you have made the way easy for it.

So we say: worship is every movement that performs a service in the universe with your intention directed to Allah.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha). Why did He single out prayer above the other acts of worship?

They said: because prayer is the constant worship that does not leave the believer as long as he has breath. Zakat, for example, falls from the poor; fasting falls from the sick; hajj falls from one who is unable. But prayer has no excuse at all that permits its abandonment: you pray standing, or sitting, or lying on your side; if you cannot, you pray by gesturing with your head or your eyelids; if you cannot, it is enough that you bring it to mind in your heart, as long as you have awareness. It never falls from you under any circumstance.

Likewise, prayer is a repeated worship: five times in the day and night, to remind you constantly of the Lord of this life if the preoccupations of life make you forget Him, and to present yourself to your Lord and Creator five times every day. And what of a machine presented to its maker in this way: can a fault or defect occur in it?

As for zakat, it is yearly or per harvest; fasting is a month in the year; hajj is once in a lifetime.

For this reason, whenever a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would stand to prayer, to present himself to his Lord and Creator, mighty and majestic. We do this in material crafts when we present the machine to its maker and engineer who knows the law of its maintenance.

In the noble hadith: "The coolness of my eyes has been made to lie in prayer."⁴

We have already mentioned that prayer has its importance, because it reminds you of your Lord five times a day, and also reminds you of yourself and of the decree of Allah concerning others, when you see the leader and his subordinate side by side in the rows of prayer. If you come before your superior, you sit in the first row, and he sits behind you; then you see him humbled and abased before Allah, the Exalted, and he knows you see him in this state, which makes him more humble with you and less haughty over you afterward.

How many people of positions and leadership have we seen weeping at the Haram, clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah and at the Multazam, he who is great, for whom people make a thousand calculations! So in prayer there is a leveling of servanthood before Allah, the Exalted.

For this reason, among the gravest afflictions suffered by Muslims is that special places in the mosque are set aside for a particular category, the place is kept empty for them, and guards accompany them even in the House of Allah; then he comes at the last moment and sits in the first row, while another spreads his prayer mat to reserve a place for him until he arrives, and finds the place empty.

The common Muslims should reject this behavior: you should move his prayer mat aside and sit yourself, for the priority of sitting is by priority of arrival, since Allah has ranked people in the mosque by their coming to it. This bad habit leads its doer into many prohibitions, as he steps over people's necks, distinguishes himself from them without right, and causes servile disparagement in the House of Allah.

And because of the importance and rank of prayer among the acts of worship, it was distinguished in its prescription in a manner suited to its importance: all acts of worship were prescribed through revelation except prayer, for the Truth summoned His true Messenger to convey it to him directly because of its importance.

We have given an example of this—and to Allah belongs the highest likeness—of a leader who, when he wants to convey a matter to his subordinate, writes to him; if the matter is important, he contacts him by telephone; if it is more important, he summons him to tell him in person. When Allah drew him near to Himself by the prescription of prayer, He made prayer a means of drawing His servants near to Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha): to establish a thing means to make it stand on firm foundations; establishing prayer is to perform it firm and complete in its pillars, not deficient.

﴿for My remembrance﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha): that is, for your remembering Me; for the constancy and monotony of blessing may make you forget the Benefactor. So when you hear the call "Allahu Akbar" and see people hastening to the houses of Allah, with no preoccupation diverting them from it, you are reminded if you were forgetful, and your heart is awakened if you were heedless.

¹ Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3585) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and its full text: "The best supplication is the supplication on the Day of 'Arafah, and the best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: there is no deity but Allah alone, without partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs the praise, and He is over all things capable." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

² hazzahu al-amr yahuzzuhu: it troubled him and weighed heavily upon him. Amr hazib and hazib: severe. In the hadith: when a matter distressed him he prayed, i.e., when a concern or grief befell him. (Lisan al-'Arab, root h-z-b)

³ On the authority of Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he prayed." Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (5/388) and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (1319).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 20, verse 15:

Then the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming – I almost conceal it – so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.﴾

That is: with what has preceded, prepare yourself, for the Hour is coming without doubt. The "Hour" here is the lifespan of the entire universe. As for the lifespans of those who dwell in the universe, they vary, each according to its term. Whoever dies, his resurrection (qiyamah) has occurred, and the matter is concluded for him.

So we say: the Hour is of two kinds. There is an hour for each of us, which is his lifespan and term, the time of which no one knows. And there is an hour for the entire universe, which is the Greater Resurrection (al-Qiyamah al-Kubra).

Concerning His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha), meaning: keep this in your mind always. Since death will carry you to it swiftly, beware lest you say: "I will die soon, but the Resurrection is after thousands or millions of years," for time is nullified after death. How so?

Time is measured only by an event; if the event ceases, time ceases too, as happens to us in sleep. Can you determine the time we slept? Therefore the Truthful, Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿As if, on the day they see it, they had not remained but an evening or its morning (46)﴾ (An-Nazi'at).

The servant whom God caused to die for a hundred years, when He raised him, said: "A day or part of a day." Likewise the People of the Cave said after three hundred years and nine, because "a day or part of a day" is the utmost that can be imagined by the sleeper when he sleeps. Therefore we say: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has occurred."[4]

Among His wisdom, Glorified is He, is that He concealed the Hour: He concealed it from the individual and concealed it from all. Perhaps if a person knew, he would say: "I will do what I want and repent before death." Therefore the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted concealed it, so that we may be on guard lest we meet God in a state of disobedience.

Likewise He concealed the Greater Hour, so that you do not take what is not yours from God's creation and benefit from it unjustly and aggressively, and so that you know that if you steal you will return to God, Who will call you to account. Since you will return to God, be upright and correct your conduct, as the people of the countryside say: "Pasture the evil ones" (ارع مساوي).

As for His saying, ﴿coming (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha), meaning: it is not brought about by anyone; it is the one that comes, although the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted is the One Who will bring it. But the meaning of "coming" is as if it were regulated automatically: when its time arrives, it occurs.

As for His saying, ﴿I almost conceal it (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha): "kad" (كاد) means "nearly," as in: "Zayd nearly came" (كاد زيد أن يجيء), i.e., he approached but has not yet come. The intended meaning is: I am about to conceal it, so no one knows its appointed time; when it occurs, we will know it. As He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him... (187)﴾ (Al-A'raf). The phrase ﴿akhfiha (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha) may also have another meaning: some triliteral verbs give the opposite of their meaning when the second letter is doubled, as in: "marida" (مرض), meaning he became ill, and "marrada" (مرّضه), meaning the physician treated him and removed his illness; and "qashartu al-shay'" (قشرت الشيء), meaning I gave it a peel, and "qashsharat al-burtuqalah" (قشّرت البرتقالة), meaning I removed its peel.

Among this is His saying: ﴿By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become ruined (harad) (85)﴾ (Yusuf). Harad means destruction, from harida, like ta'iba.

And His saying: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight (65)﴾ (Al-Anfal).

The meaning of "harrida" (حرّض) is urging them to fight, which removes destruction from them before the disbelievers; for if they do not strive, they will be destroyed. So "harida" means he was destroyed, and "harrada" means he removed destruction.

Sometimes the opposite of a verb comes by adding a hamzah to the verb, as in: ﴿As for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell (15)﴾ (Al-Jinn). The qasit (القاسط) is from qasata, meaning the one who is unjust through disbelief.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, God loves the just (muqsitin) (42)﴾ (Al-Ma'idah): the muqsit, from aqsata, is the just one who removes injustice. Although the root is one, qasata, the verbal nouns differ: we say qasata qistan, meaning he was just, and qasata qasatan and qusuwwan, meaning he was unjust. This hamzah in aqsata is called hamzat al-izalah (the hamzah of removal).

From the triliteral verb qasata come al-qist (justice) and al-mizan (the balance). The difference between qasata and aqsata: qasata means he was just from the outset and from the very beginning, whereas aqsata means that when he found an injustice he lifted it and removed it; so he added to justice that he removed oppression.

Also the verb 'ajama: 'ajama al-amr means he concealed the matter, and a'jamahu means he removed its concealment. From this comes the word mu'jam, which removes the concealment of words and clarifies them.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿I almost conceal it... (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha): khafiya means he hid himself, and akhfaha means he removed its concealment; and the concealment of a thing is removed only by announcing it.

Then He, Exalted, says: ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives (15)﴾ (Ta-Ha):

Were there no reckoning and recompense in the Hereafter, those who wasted themselves and ran wild in existence would have more fortune than the believers committed to God's method. Therefore, in our discussion with the communists, we said to them: "You have killed those of your enemies, the capitalists, whom you overtook; but what of the one who died and whom you did not overtake? And how do these escape from you?"

It was more fitting for you to believe in another place from which these do not escape, where they receive their recompense: it is the Hereafter, in which every soul is recompensed for what it strives.

1 Here it is mentioned without the emphatic lam. In Surah Ghafir, however, He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt in it... (59)﴾ (Ghafir), with the emphatic lam, because the addressees in Surah Ghafir are the disbelievers, so the report needed emphasis. (Fath al-Rahman bi-kashf ma yaltabis fi al-Qur'an by Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari, p. 260), with adaptation.

2 This is 'Uzayr, peace be upon him. Concerning him God said: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was fallen upon its roofs. He said, "How will God bring this to life after its death?" So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day..." (259)﴾ (Al-Baqarah).

3 Concerning this God says: ﴿And thus We raised them that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day..." (19)﴾ (Al-Kahf).

4 Al-Ajluni mentioned it in Kashf al-Khafa' (hadith no. 2618) from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, and its completion is: "Remember death often, for if you remember it in prosperity, it will sour it for you, and if you remember it in hardship, it will widen it for you. Death is the Resurrection."

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿So let not those who do not believe in it, and who follow their own desires, turn you away from it, lest you perish.﴾

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is giving Musa (peace be upon him) immunity against what the disbelievers will say, those who cast doubt on the Hereafter and fear it. Their aim is for this to be a lie, for the Hereafter is not in their interest, and their share is to deny it.

So beware of listening to them when they turn you away from it. They say: ﴿When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? Or our forefathers of old?﴾ (al-Saffat).

And why do these people find it unlikely? Is not the One who created them from nothing able to restore them after they have become bones?

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him.﴾ (al-Rum)

This is an analogy suited to your understanding and to what you have become accustomed to among "easy" and "easier." As for the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, there is nothing easier or more difficult for Him, because His command is between the "Kaf" and the "Nun" (i.e., His saying "Be" and it is).

But why do the disbelievers turn away from the Hereafter and belief in it? Because they know that they will be recompensed for what they have done, and this is a difficult matter for them, and it is in their interest that the Hereafter be a lie.

Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri spoke truly when he said:
"The astrologer and the physician both claim
that bodies will not be gathered. I say to you both:
If your saying is true, I have lost nothing,
but if my saying is true, the loss is upon you both."

That is: the believer in resurrection, if he does not gain, will not lose, whereas you, O deniers, are the losers.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus perish﴾ (Ta-Ha), meaning: perish, from al-radaa, which is destruction.

Thus the address from Allah, exalted is He, to Musa (peace be upon him) came first with the beginning: belief in Allah alone, with no partner, and this is the first summit. Then He brought the final summit, which is resurrection. So the matter is, therefore, from Him as a beginning and to Him as an end: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me...﴾ (14) (Ta-Ha), until He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it...﴾ (15) (Ta-Ha).

Thereafter, the Truth (Exalted is He) explained to us the beginning of His revelation to His Messenger Musa (peace be upon him)(1).

مَا (mā): interrogative. The taa' after it indicates a feminine thing, which is what Musa is holding in his hand, and the kaaf is for address, as if He had said to him: "What is that thing in your hand?" The answer to this question is completed with one word: "a staff" (ʿaṣā).

As for Musa (peace be upon him), he knows that it is Allah Most High who is asking, and what is in his hand is not hidden from Him. But this is a speech of intimacy (ʾīnās), because the situation is difficult, and his Lord wants to reassure him and put him at ease.

When the intimacy comes from Allah, the servant should seize this opportunity and prolong the enjoyment of companionship with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and not cut off the conversation with a single word. Therefore Musa (peace be upon him) responded:

﴿He said, "It is my staff. I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."﴾ (20:18)

(1) Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari said in his book Fath al-Rahman (p. 260): "If you say: What is the benefit of Allah's question to Musa, when He knows better than anyone what is in his hand? I say: its benefit is to put him at ease and to lighten the awe that came over him at the moment of the address and the majesty of speaking with Him; or to have him acknowledge that it is a staff, and to increase his knowledge of that, so that when Allah turns it into a serpent he will not doubt that it was a staff which then became a serpent by the power of Allah Most High."

Musa said: ﴿It is my staff⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha), then he opens for himself another avenue of speech: ﴿I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha). Here Musa sees that he has gone on and added too much, so he tries to be brief: ﴿And I have in it other uses⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha).

Musa was waiting for a question, which would say: "And what are these uses?", so that he could prolong his intimacy with his Lord. When the address is with Allah, none ends it except one who is indifferent to Allah.

The staff has a long history with mankind. It is a necessity for discipline and training, a necessity for journeys, and it has its importance in herding... etc. Here Musa – peace be upon him – mentions some of these benefits, saying:

﴿I lean upon it⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha), i.e., I rely on it and support myself when I walk. A person needs to lean on a staff when walking and when tired, because he needs two kinds of strength: strength for movement and walking, and strength to bear the body. The staff helps him bear the weight of his body, especially if he is tired and his feet cannot bear him.

So his saying ﴿I lean upon it⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha) means: I rely on it while walking and while I stand to graze the sheep, so I support myself on it. Leaning alternates a person's weight between his feet, so it rests the foot that has become tired, and he shifts from one side to the other.

When a person's body rests on one thing for a long time, the pores of the body in that place become blocked and do not allow sweat to be released, and this causes serious harm, which we see in patients who remain bedridden for a long time. This harm appears in the form of an ulcer they call "bedsore." Therefore doctors advise such patients to change their position, so that they do not lie on one side only.

For this reason, the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, decreed that the People of the Cave be turned in their sleep from side to side, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left⁠﴾ (Al-Kahf).

Therefore, when a person stands for a long time, or sits for a long time without finding a support to lean on, you see him restless and unsettled. From here, the reclining support has been one of the signs of blessing and luxury in this world and in the Hereafter, as the Exalted said concerning the wife of the ʿAziz: ﴿And she prepared for them a banquet/couch⁠﴾ (Yusuf).

And He said about the bliss of the Hereafter: ﴿Reclining on thrones arranged in rows⁠﴾ (At-Tur).

And He said: ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful carpets⁠﴾ (Ar-Rahman).

And the Truth, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Reclining on green rafraf and beautiful ʿabqari⁠﴾ (Ar-Rahman).

So leaning is a means of comfort, and a person should change his support from side to side so that he is not exposed to what is called "bedsore."
