1 Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/328), and Muslim in his Sahih (1015), Kitab al-Zakat, and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2989), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.
2 Al-Risha': the rope. Arshā al-dalw: he gave the bucket a rishā', that is, a rope. (Lisan al-Arab, root r-sh-w). Ibn Manzur mentioned this condition in (Lisan al-Arab, root h-w-y), saying: (Ibn Barri said: al-Riyashi reported from Abu Zayd that al-hawa with a fatha on the ha' is downward, and with a damma it is upward).

Ghaffar: an intensive form (sigha mubalagha) of ghafara. When the intensive is affirmed, the linguistic order establishes the lesser meaning, which is ghafir (forgiver). This applies to affirmation. Likewise in negation, as in His saying ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]: He negated intensive injustice. Does that mean that He, blessed and exalted, could be unjust?

Something may be intensified in two ways. The first: you intensify the act itself, as when one eats one loaf in a meal or two, and another eats five loaves. This is intensification in the act itself, which is eating. The second: intensification may be by repetition of the act. The custom is to eat three times, and there are those who eat six meals, and we call such a person (akkul), meaning one who eats much, not in a single meal but in the number of meals.

So the meaning of (ghaffar) is: forgiving to me, forgiving to you, forgiving to this one and that one, forgiving to all creation. Thus His forgiveness, mighty and majestic, to His creation is repeated.

The Truthful, glorified and exalted, has legislated forgiveness and repentance in order to protect societies from their wicked members. When the evildoer commits a crime and finds no opportunity for forgiveness and repentance, he grows accustomed to crime and even intensifies it.

But when the door of repentance and forgiveness is opened to him, this spares society from the savagery of people of evil.

God, mighty and majestic, is not only a forgiver of sins; He is ghaffar of them. Whenever you return to Him, He forgives you. But resolve within yourself that when you commit a sin and repent of it, you will not return to it, and do not arrange and plan your disobedience on the hope that you will repent. For what do you know, perhaps you will not live to repent?

Forgiveness is for ﴿those who repent and believe..﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]. Since He said ﴿repents and believes..﴾, the repentance here must be from disbelief, and then he creates faith in God and His Messenger. Faith is the wellspring from which human conduct issues, and this requires that you hear His words, carry out His commands, and avoid His prohibitions. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds..﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82].

But, is righteous action not guidance? Why then did He say after it ﴿then is guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]? They said: because guidance means that you persist in this righteous action and seek to increase in it, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance..﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

1 Said by Sufyan al-Thawri, Qatada and others; al-Qurtubi mentioned it in his tafsir (6/4404) and after it mentioned seven other sayings:
That is, he did not doubt his faith. Said by Ibn Abbas; mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi.
He adhered to the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. Also said by Ibn Abbas; mentioned by al-Tha'labi.
He took the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ). Said by Anas; mentioned by al-Mahdawi.
He did the deed correctly. Said by Ibn Zayd; mentioned by al-Mahdawi.
He learned knowledge so that he would be guided how to act. Said by Ibn Zayd.
He knew that there is reward for it and punishment for neglecting it. Said by al-Sha'bi, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.
He was guided in the wilayah of the People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ). Said by Thabit al-Bunani.
Then al-Qurtubi said: "The first saying is the best of these sayings, God willing, and all the others return to it."

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾

We say: "What hastened you?" means: how quickly did you come? Why did you arrive before your appointed time? Musa (peace be upon him) had an appointment with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, to receive the method (al-manhaj) from Him. It was expected that at this meeting he would come with a group of the choicest of his people and their leaders. But Musa hastened ahead of his Lord's appointment and went on without his people. So He said to him: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ (Ta-Ha), meaning: you hurried ahead and came without them.

Footnote 1: Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4406): "Some said: by 'the people' he meant the seventy whom he chose, and Musa, when he drew near to the Mount (al-Tur), outran them out of longing to hear the speech of Allah." And the Exalted has said: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment. Then when the earthquake seized them, he said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before and me. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?..."﴾ (al-A'raf) (155).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 84:

Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿They are following in my footsteps, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be well-pleased.﴾

That is: they are coming after me and will follow me. As for me, ﴿I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be well-pleased﴾ (Ta-Ha): I hastened to stand before You, that You may be pleased.

Musa hastened to the appointed meeting with his Lord and went ahead of his people for a wisdom. When a person orders others to do something that is burdensome to the self and restricts its desires, he must begin with himself. He says: I am not exempt from this matter; rather, I am the first to carry out what I command you, and I will go ahead of you to it.

Thus the conquering commander Tariq ibn Ziyad (1) said to his soldiers: (Know that when the two hosts meet, I will advance myself against the tyrant of the people, Lazriq, and fight him, God willing; if I kill him, you will have been spared his affair.) This is how leadership becomes an example and a model, as they say in proverbs: "Do such-and-such, and my hand is in your hand." Here he says: my hand before yours.

So Musa (peace be upon him) says: ﴿and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be well-pleased﴾ (Ta-Ha): that You may be pleased that Your method is being applied on my part, as a trusted messenger charged with it, and on the part of my people, because when they see me having hastened to meet You at the appointed time, they will know that there is good for them in that; otherwise I would not have gone ahead of them to it. Thereby God's method prevails and is established on earth. And when God's method prevails, God is pleased with His vicegerent on earth.

(1) He is Tariq ibn Ziyad al-Laythi by clientage, the conqueror of al-Andalus. He was originally of the Berbers, and embraced Islam at the hand of Musa ibn Nusayr, and became one of his most valiant men. He was born around 50 AH and penetrated deep into the land of al-Andalus. He died in the year 102 AH. (al-A'lam by al-Zirikli, 3/217).

Then Allah, exalted is He, informs His Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) of what occurred among his people after he had parted from them, namely the matter of worshipping the calf. ﴿He said, "Indeed We have tested your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾

Al-fitna (trial, test): In itself it is not blameworthy, because fitna means examination and testing, and its outcome is what is praised or blamed. It is like a student who sits an examination: if he succeeds, this is good for him, and if he fails, this is good for people. How so?

They say: there are matters where, if the benefit of the individual is realised, the benefit of the community collapses. If the negligent, lazy student were able to pass without studying and without effort, he would have gained a personal benefit, albeit a foolish one, but he would give others a signal, suggest to them that responsibility is unnecessary, and spread frustration and apathy in society, and that alone is enough of a loss for society.

The word fitna has come in this sense in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ (al-'Ankabut, 29:2).

Therefore, testing is necessary so that each person is given according to his outcome. If someone asks: "Does Allah test His servants in order to know their condition?" We say: rather, He tests so that people may know their condition, and their true natures are revealed, so that they deal with them on that basis: this one is a hypocrite, this one is sincere, this one is a liar, and you can then take precautions in dealing with them.

Therefore: the testing is not so that Allah may know, but so that the creatures of Allah may know.

Or: testing from Allah is to establish the proof against the one being tested. For example, one may say: "If Allah had given me wealth, I would spend it in such and such good ways." But when he is placed in a real test and given wealth, he holds back and is stingy. And if Allah had left him without wealth, he would have said: "If I had had it, I would have done such and such."

So there is a knowledge that actually exists with Allah, or a knowledge among the creatures of Allah for everyone who is tested: if he is a good person, they follow him, turn to him, love him and listen to him; otherwise they turn away from him. Thus the purpose of testing is the community and its well-being.

Allah, glorified is He, called what happened among the Children of Israel during Musa's absence, namely the worship of the calf, a fitna, and then attributed it to Himself: ﴿We have tested...﴾ (Ta-Ha, 20:85), that is, We tested them.

Then He says: ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ (Ta-Ha, 20:85). Adalla (to lead astray): he led them along a path other than the path of truth. Leading along a path other than the truth may be purely personal, in which case a person bears only his own burden, and it may extend to others, so that he leads them onto the path of error, in which case he bears his own burden and the burden of those he led astray.

On this matter Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they lead astray without knowledge...﴾ (al-Nahl, 16:25).

Yet Allah, exalted is He, also says in another verse: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another...﴾ (Fatir, 35:18).

This is one of the matters at which some Orientalists paused, trying to accuse the Qur'an and its style of contradiction. This was only because of their failure to understand the language of the Qur'an and their treating it as a craft rather than an innate faculty. Had they understood the Qur'an, they would have known the difference between a person going astray in himself and a person being the cause of others' going astray.

Al-Samiri(1): his name was Musa al-Samiri. It is narrated that his mother placed him in a desert with no life in it, then she died in childbirth, so the child remained without a mother to care for him, and Jibril (peace be upon him) used to attend to him and raise him until he grew up(2).

The poet expressed this scene and the contrasts it contains between Musa (peace be upon him) and Musa al-Samiri, saying:
If you do not find care among your sons,
then the hopeful one has lied and the aspirer has failed.
Musa, whom Jibril raised, is a disbeliever,
and Musa, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger.

1. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Samiri was from a people who worshipped cows. He came to the land of Egypt and entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what it contained of worshipping cows. It was also said that he was a man of the Copts, a neighbour of Musa who believed in him and went out with him. It was also said that he was a great man among the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe known as the Samaritans, who are known in the Levant. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi, 6/4407).

2. Ibn 'Abbas said, concerning Allah's words about al-Samiri: ﴿He said, "I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger..."﴾ (Ta-Ha, 20:96): al-Samiri recognised Jibril, because his mother, when she feared he would be slaughtered, hid him in a cave and sealed it over him, and Jibril would come to him and nourish him with his fingers: in one finger milk, in another honey, and in another ghee. He continued to nourish him until he grew up, and when he saw him at the sea he recognised him.

Then Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?"﴾

Raja'a (returned): it is used intransitively, as in raja'a fulan ila al-haqq (so-and-so returned to the truth), and transitively, as in ﴿Then if Allah returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out...﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:83). The meaning differs between the two uses.

Here, "Moses returned" means that when he heard what had happened to his people through the trial of the Samiri. ﴿Angry and grieved﴾ (20:86) means: deeply saddened by what had occurred.

﴿Did your Lord not make you a good promise?﴾ (20:86): the good promise is that Allah would give them the Torah, in which are the foundations of the movement of life, through which our life in this world is made good and our reward in the Hereafter is made good.

As for His saying, ﴿Did the time seem long to you?﴾ (20:86), it means: my absence from you was prolonged, and so it became distant enough that you forgot it, though I had been away from you only a short period. Allah said about it: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten...﴾ (al-A'raf 7:142).

Then He says: ﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?﴾ (20:86).

Since my covenant with you is recent, and forgetfulness has not yet occurred in it, you must have intended disobedience and sought the wrath of Allah. Otherwise the matter would not warrant this. By merely being absent from you for a moment you suffer this relapse. And if this is the state of the people while their Messenger is still among them, what then will be their state after his death?

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Such a thing while I am still among you?"

That is: what is this that is happening from you while I am still present among you?

As for His saying, ﴿so that you broke your promise to me﴾ (20:86), and in another verse He said: ﴿Evil is what you did as my successors after me﴾ (al-A'raf 7:150): it seems that there was a promise and an agreement between him and them. Before he left them he had charged them to follow the way of Harun and to obey his commands until he returned to them. Harun was the one who would succeed him among his people after him, and he was his partner in the prophethood, and he held the dignity of the Messenger, so obedience to him was obligatory.

This is the promise they broke with their prophet Moses (peace be upon him). ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you of our own will, but we were loaded with burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus the Samiri cast [them]."﴾ (20:87)

1 Al-Nasa'i reported in his Sunan (6/142), in the Book of Divorce, from the hadith of Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed about a man who had divorced his wife with three pronouncements at once, so he stood up angry and said: "Is the Book of Allah being played with while I am still among you?" until a man stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I not kill him?"

The root (m-l-k) has three forms, each with its own meaning, and they are not synonyms with one meaning, as some claim. Malaka (with a fatha on the mim) and malika (with a kasra) and mulka (with a damma) all express possession and ownership. However, malaka means a person's control over himself, his essence and his will, without his owning anything else around him.

Malika (with a kasra) means to possess what is outside your own self.

Mulk (with a damma) means that you own something, and you own it as one who possesses it.

So these three are not synonyms with one meaning. Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you by our own will (bi-maliknā)..﴾ (Ta-Ha: 87). That is: by our own will; rather, there were other matters outside our will that compelled us to break the promise. So what are these matters that were outside your will?

They said: ﴿But we were loaded with burdens of the ornaments of the people..﴾ (Ta-Ha: 87).

"Awzār" is the plural of wizr, which is a thing heavy upon the soul. The word wizr is used for sin, because it is heavy upon the soul, a heaviness that extends into the Hereafter as well, where the pain of the burden does not end. Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection, a burden (himl)..﴾ (Ta-Ha: 101).

These burdens were from the ornaments of the people, that is, the people of Pharaoh. It is said that during their festivals they would borrow jewelry from their neighbours and acquaintances among the people of Pharaoh, and adorn themselves with it. Then why did they not return these trusts to their owners before going out to the appointed meeting to which he had promised them?

They said: because they wanted to conceal the hour of their departure so that their enemies would not prepare against them and prevent them from leaving; so they hurried and had no time to return them.

Some people said: these adornments and jewelry were among what the sea threw up after Pharaoh and his people drowned. But this view is rejected, because if they took them after the sea had cast them up, they would be spoils (aslāb), not burdens (awzār).

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So we threw them, and thus did the Samiri cast..﴾ (Ta-Ha: 87).

When the word "zina" (adornment) is used without qualification, it usually refers to gold. Qadhf (throwing) is hurling forcefully, as if the thrower is disgusted at having to carry what he throws. This indicates that the Children of Israel still had a leaven of faith among them, so they felt pain and grief because they had not returned the trusts to their rightful owners.

For this reason, al-Samiri entered upon them from this direction, and made them understand: you will not be freed from this disobedience except by throwing this adornment into the fire(1), while he intended something else, namely that the gold would melt and the impurities in it would come out. ﴿Thus did al-Samiri cast..﴾ (Ta-Ha: 87): that is, he cast what he had of jewelry. But there is a difference between qadhf and ilqa'; ilqa' (casting) carries gentleness and deliberation, for he was their leader and teacher.

(1) Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir (6/4408), cited something similar from the statement of Qatadah: when the people were slow in returning from Musa, al-Samiri said to them: "He has only been delayed on your account because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it to al-Samiri, who threw it into the fire, and fashioned from it a calf for them, then cast upon it a handful from the hoofprint of the Messenger, who was Jibril, peace be upon him..

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿So he brought forth for them a calf, a body that lowed⁽¹⁾. Then they said, "This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten."﴾ (20:88)

That is, he brought forth for them, from this molten gold, ﴿a calf, a body...﴾ (20:88). The word "jasad" (body) also occurs in the Qur'an in the story of Solomon (peace be upon him), where the Exalted says: ﴿And We did try Solomon, and We placed upon his throne a body; then he turned in repentance﴾ (38:34).

Allah had given Solomon a mighty kingdom such as should not belong to anyone after him. He subjected to him the birds, the jinn, and mankind, and the wind, which moved at his command. It seems that some pride or conceit overtook him, so the Truth, glorified is He, wished to draw his attention to the Giver of this kingdom and to remind him that this kingdom does not subsist by itself, but only by the command of Allah, who is able to make you sit upon your throne as a body with no movement in it and no power even over its own limbs and self.

As you see the man – God forbid – who has been struck by total paralysis that has left him a body with no movement and no will over his limbs. If he has no will over a single one of his limbs, will he have will over what is outside him, of birds, humans, or jinn?

So do not be deceived that Allah has made you commander over all the kinds, for He is able to strip you of all of this.

It is narrated⁽²⁾ that Solomon, peace be upon him, rode the flying carpet, which carried him wherever he wished, as the Exalted says: ﴿And to Solomon the wind: its morning course was a month's journey, and its evening course a month's journey﴾ (34:12). Then something of pride and conceit entered him, and he heard someone beneath him say: "O Solomon" – thus without titles – "we were commanded to obey you only so long as you obey Allah." Then he returned him to where he had been. Therefore Solomon, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness and turned in repentance.

Likewise we see that when a person dies, the first thing to be forgotten is his name. They say: "The corpse, the corpse! Here: what have you done with the corpse?" Then this too is forgotten the moment he is placed in his coffin, and they say: "The wood! Where is the wood now? Wait for the wood..." Glory be to Allah! The moment the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, takes His spirit from the servant, he becomes a corpse, and becomes wood. What is this world whose end is like this?

As for His words: ﴿a calf, a body that lowed﴾ (20:88), that is, there is no movement in it; it is merely an image, fashioned in a particular form so that when the wind strikes it, it produces a whistling sound resembling the lowing (khuwar), that is, the voice of cattle.

But why did the Samiri think this way and choose the matter of the calf?

It is said: because the Samiri exploited the longing of the Children of Israel and their inclination toward idolatry and paganism, which were deeply rooted in them. Did they not say to their prophet, peace be upon him, while their feet were still wet from the sea after Allah had delivered them from Pharaoh, and it was fitting for them to thank Allah, yet they said when they came upon a people devoting themselves to idols of theirs: ﴿O Moses, make for us a god as they have gods﴾ (7:138).

So he brought them this calf, having advanced it beyond mere idolatry: he made it a body and gave it a lowing, an audible voice.

Then He says: ﴿Then they said, "This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten"﴾ (20:88), that is: the Samiri forgot the leaven of faith within himself, and forgot that this deed was a departure from faith into disbelief. Would that he had disbelieved only in himself; rather he disbelieved and caused people to disbelieve. He must have forgotten, for had he been mindful of faith, and of the consequence of his deed and the ruin of what he undertook, he would not have done what he did.⁽³⁾

¹ Al-khuwar: the lowing of a bull and the strong sound of a calf or cow; one says "kharra yakhoru," meaning he cried out. (Lisan al-Arab, root kh-w-r.)

² Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi narrated in a report from Malik, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Solomon, peace be upon him, used to ride the wind from Istakhr, lunch in Bayt al-Maqdis, then return and dine in Istakhr. Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/677).

³ Another interpretation has been given of this verse, mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4409) and Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/162). Its import is that it is a statement of the Samiri about Moses: that he went astray and went off seeking his god, while he is here. And from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: (i.e., "Moses forgot to tell you that He is his god").

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them, and possesses for them no harm nor benefit?﴾ (89).

Meaning: How can they worship this calf, when it does not answer them with a reply, nor possess anything for them? Just as He, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham (69) when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?" (70) They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them." (71) He said, "Do they hear you when you call (on them)? (72) Or do they benefit you or harm you?" (73)﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara).

Whoever has even an atom of intellect would not proceed with this matter; therefore, the Truthful, glory be to Him, debates these people: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah...? (28)﴾ (Al-Baqarah).

Meaning: Tell us the path that leads you to disbelief, as if it were a strange matter that reason neither accepts nor approves. Did it not occur to those who worshipped the calf that it does not answer them if they ask it, nor possess harm for them if they disbelieve in it, nor benefit if they believe in it and worship it?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 90:

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it. Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."﴾

Harun (peace be upon him) was the successor (khalifah) of his brother during his absence, as the Exalted said: ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ (al-A'raf)

"Take my place and do what is good." This was a delegation from Musa to his brother Harun to judge among the people as he saw fit and to weigh what was beneficial as he judged. This delegation later served as intercession (shafa'a) for Harun before his brother.

So the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it..."﴾ (Ta-Ha)

Thus Harun admonished them to the extent of his ability, and made clear to them that this matter of the calf was a trial from Allah. In this affair his judgment was not to enter into battle with these people, because the people were three hundred thousand in all, and twelve thousand of them worshipped the calf. Had Harun (peace be upon him) turned it into a battle, he would have annihilated all of that number.

Therefore he limited himself to admonition: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it. Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command.﴾ (Ta-Ha), just as you had taken the covenant before Musa.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 91:

﴿Lan nabraha..(91)﴾ (Taha): That is: we will remain in this state. Some think that it (the verb "yabrah," to depart or cease) refers only to place, but it depends on what it is connected with. You say: "I will not cease traveling until I reach my goal" (lā abraḥu sā'iran ḥattā aṣila li-gharḍī), and "I will not cease this place" (lā abraḥu hādhā al-makān). It may be used for place, and it may be used for state. As occurs in the Qur'an:

- For place and residence, in His saying: ﴿So I will never leave the land until my father permits me..(80)﴾ (Yusuf).

- For state, in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when Musa said to his young man, "I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas..(60)﴾ (al-Kahf), meaning: I will not cease traveling.

So the meaning of ﴿We will never cease to be devoted to it..(91)﴾ (Taha) is: we will remain at its worship until Musa returns, for we will not remain this period without a god.

Then the Truthful (Allah, glory be to Him) says: ﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,﴾ [20:92].

This is a dialogue that took place between Musa and his brother Harun. ﴿What prevented you...﴾ [20:92] (Ta-Ha): This expression has come in the Qur'an in two styles. The first is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating...﴾ [38:75] (Sad), meaning: what prevented you from prostrating.

The other is: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating...﴾ [7:12] (al-A'raf), meaning: what prevented you from not prostrating. This is because the preventer may be a compulsion upon you, while you do not want to do it, and another may come and persuade you to do it. So at one time he compels you: you do not want to prostrate, and he says to you: "Prostrate!" Therefore, "What prevented you from prostrating" means he compelled you against your will; but if he persuaded you to prostrate by your own choice, then he has prevented you from not prostrating.

So, at times the prevention comes from the self, and at times from others, and thus the two styles meet.

As for His saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you then disobey my command?﴾ [20:92-93] (Ta-Ha): meaning: from following me. But does Musa, peace be upon him, here seek information? In reality he does not intend a question. You may address a person about a fault while you do not know his fault; you address him in the form of a fault only so that you hear his answer, and so that it is a reply to one who objects to him.

From this is what occurred with our master Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, at the Black Stone: when he kissed it he said: "O Allah, I know that you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits, and had I not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissing you, I would not have kissed you."(1)

So Umar kissed it because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissed it; however, he uttered these words to give us a lasting answer, throughout history, to everyone who asks about kissing the Stone.

Here, Musa raised this doubt so that we would hear the answer, and hear the reply from the one concerned, remaining and continuing throughout the ages.

1. Related by Imam Muslim in his Sahih (1270), Book of Hajj. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary: (He only said "and you neither harm nor benefit" so that some who were recently converted to Islam, who had become accustomed to worshipping stones and glorifying them and hoping for their benefit, would not be deceived.)

This is a dialogue that took place between Musa (Moses) and his brother Harun (Aaron). ﴿What prevented you...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:92). This expression occurs in the Qur'an in two styles. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating...﴾ (Sad 38:75), meaning: what prevented you from prostrating?

The second is: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating...﴾ (al-A'raf 7:12), meaning: what prevented you from not prostrating? For the one who prevents you may be compelling you against your will while you do not want to act, or another may come and persuade you to act. So sometimes he forces you: you do not want to prostrate, and he says to you, "Prostrate!" Thus, "What prevented you from prostrating" means that he compelled you against your will; but if he persuades you to prostrate of your own choice, then he has prevented you from not prostrating.

So, sometimes the prevention comes from the self, and sometimes from another; and thus the two styles meet.

As for His saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, (92) from following me? Did you then disobey my command?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:92-93), meaning: from following me. But does Musa, peace be upon him, here ask a question? In reality, he does not intend a question. You may address a person about a fault while you do not know his fault; you address him in the form of a fault so that you may hear his answer from him, and so that it becomes a reply to one who objects to him.

From this is what happened with our master Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, at the Black Stone: when he kissed it, he said: "O Allah, I know that you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits, and had I not seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissing you, I would not have kissed you."(1)

So Umar kissed it because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissed it; but he uttered these words to give us a lasting answer, throughout history, to everyone who asks about kissing the Black Stone.

Here, Musa raised a doubt so that we may hear the answer, and so that we may hear the reply from the one concerned, remaining and continuing throughout the ages.

1 Related by Imam Muslim in his Sahih (1270), Book of Hajj. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary: (He only said, "and that you neither harm nor benefit," lest some of those recently converted to Islam, who had been accustomed to worshipping stones and venerating them and hoping for their benefit, be deceived.)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 94:

Idhan (so, then): the one who addressed Musa's brother Harun is an act of impulse and movement, which we understand from Harun's words: ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard nor by my head.﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:94).

Then he mentioned the reason: ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:94), meaning his brother's saying: ﴿Take my place among my people and act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.﴾ (al-A'raf 7:142).

He mentioned the delegation (tafwid) that Musa had given him. Harun had exerted himself (ijtihad) according to his view of the situation, and he kept the people away from a battle that might have ended with the elimination of the seed of faith among the Children of Israel. He exerted himself within the framework of ﴿and act righteously﴾ (al-A'raf 7:142).

Idhan (so, then): Musa raised this matter with his brother, not so that he would hear the reply himself, but so that the whole world would hear it throughout history.

Then Moses turns the address to the head of this trial:

﴿He said, "What is your affair, O Samiri?" (95)﴾.

That is: what is your situation, and what is your story?

Al-khatb (the grave matter, lit. "affair"): it is said of a significant event which people call a grave occurrence (ḥadath jallal), and of which it is said "khatb." It is not a passing matter that no one pauses over.

Among the instances of this is the Almighty's saying: ﴿"What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?..." (51)﴾ (Yusuf).

And what the Qur'an relates of Moses' saying (peace be upon him) to the two daughters of Shu'ayb: ﴿"What is your affair?..." (23)﴾ (al-Qasas).

1 Rawada 'ala al-shay' murawada: he sought it from him with effort, cunning and bargaining. As for the Almighty's saying ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself...﴾ (Yusuf 23): that is, her self sought from him through attempt and deception, so that he would overstep and descend from the pride, nobility and chastity of his self; it is a metaphor for seeking sexual intercourse. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/281).

Then the Exalted says about the Samiri: ﴿He said, "I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away. Thus did my soul prompt me."﴾

Root: بصر (baṣara). Its form أبصرت is used for sensory sight, while بصرت is used for knowing, i.e., meaning "I knew."

As for the meaning of ﴿I saw what they did not see﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): it means: I was convinced of their matter while they were not convinced by it. I acted, and they followed me in what I did regarding the calf affair.

His own ijtihad (independent reasoning) led him to fashion the calf, because he saw his people loving idols. They had earlier asked Musa to make for them a god when they saw a people worshipping idols. So the Samiri seized the opportunity of Musa's absence and said to them: "I will make for you what Musa could not make. Indeed, I will even add to it. You asked only for a mere idol of stone; I will make for you a calf of gold, a body with a voice and an audible lowing."

As for his words ﴿so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): qabada ʿala al-shay' means he took it by gathering his hand around it. Similar to it is qabaṣa (with ṣād).[2]

As for his words ﴿from the footprint of the Messenger﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): scholars have various reports on this matter. Among them: that when Jibril (peace be upon him) was nurturing him as a child, he would come to him on a steed, and the Samiri noticed that whenever the steed passed over something, the place of its hoof turned green and life stirred in it. Therefore, the proponents of this view hold that the calf was real and had a natural voice, not merely the passing of wind through it.[3]

Another opinion says: ﴿the footprint of the Messenger﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): the Messenger, as we know, is the one who conveys the law of God directly to the one he conveys it to; Jibril, however, is the messenger of the Messenger, and no one saw him. So the term "Messenger" was applied to the bearer of the method to the one who speaks it. But it may also be used with the intent of mockery, as in His words: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God..."﴾ (al-Munafiqun 7), where they say "the Messenger of God" mockingly, not in belief in it.

Likewise in His words: ﴿And they said, "What is this Messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ (al-Furqan 7).

Thus, it may be intended as mockery.

But what is meant by the footprint of the Messenger? The Messenger came to convey a law from God, and this is his footprint that remains after him. So the meaning is: I took a handful from the law of the Messenger, a handful from its summit, which is the matter of the one, unique God who is worshipped, not an idol or anything else.

As for His words ﴿and I threw it away﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): that is, I cast it away and removed it from my imagination, then I gave free rein to my soul to think about what lies beyond this.

The proof is that He said after it: ﴿Thus did my soul prompt me﴾ (Ta-Ha 96): that is, it adorned it for me and drove me to disobedience. One does not say "my soul prompted me to obedience"; rather, it is disobedience, namely that he takes something from the footprint of the Messenger and his revelation which came from God, then discards it from his method and removes it from his thought, then walks by his own free choice.

[1] Nabadha al-shay': he threw it and cast it away. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/251). And al-nabdh: your casting of a thing from your hand in front of you or behind you. (Lisan al-Arab, root نبذ).
[2] This is a reading of al-Hasan al-Basri. Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan that he would read it (fa-qabaṣtu) with ṣād, and he said: al-qabṣ is with the fingertips. (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 5/596).
[3] For this reason they said: the meaning of ﴿fa-qabadtu qabḍatan min athari al-rasul﴾ (96) (Ta-Ha) is: from the footprint of his horse. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/163): "This is the well-known view among many exegetes, or most of them."

Then the Truthful (Allah, glorified is He) says:

﴿He said, "Then go; for you, in this life, it is that you will say, 'No touching,' and you have a appointment that you will not be able to break. And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then scatter it into the sea, a [complete] scattering."﴾ (20:97)

The response of Musa, peace be upon him, to this deed of the Samiri was: your recompense is that you go away, and your saying that will remain with you is: ﴿No touching...﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha). And al-massas (المساس) means al-mass (touching). The meaning admits of two readings: "No touching by me of anyone," or "No touching of me by anyone."

That is because those who fabricate lies and claim that they have a message and the mission of the prophets, their share of all this is that they should have worldly authority and a standing in people's hearts, and that they should have a doctrine, followers and partisans.

Therefore you always see them, in pursuit of this goal, slipping away from the true method and replacing it with methods according to their desires, so they lean towards making the method easy and simplified, and they give their followers a freedom for which Allah has sent down no authority, like the one who came out to us permitting people to mix between men and women.

And it is strange that you find supporters of these ideas who believe in them and apply them, not from the common people, but from the intellectuals and holders of positions. So how can women be veiled from them, when she is half of society?

So: how beautiful this religion is, and how easy for people! It has come in accordance with their desires and their appetites, and it has widened matters for them. The soul by its nature inclines to religiosity, because it was created upon it, but it wants this religion to be easy, without hardship in it, even if it opposes the method of Allah.

Therefore you find, for example, Musaylima and Sajah and others of those who claim prophethood lightening for their followers the burdens of the Law in prayer and fasting, while zakat is heavy upon the soul, so there is no need for it; otherwise what distinction did they bring for people to follow them? And what means of encouragement are there to follow the new religion?

Thus these people come to have worldly authority and standing, and followers and a mass audience. So: whoever has ruined his life, seeking glory and standing in people's submission and following of his ideas, Allah punishes him through them, and makes his humiliation at their hands and his trial from their side. They are the ones who helped him in this falsehood; then he hates them and keeps himself away from them, to the degree that he says: ﴿No touching...﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha), as if he flees from them, saying: beware lest you come near me or touch me.

Nearness and love have turned into distance and enmity. This crowd that was around him, and in which lay his glory and dominance, he now flees from; they are the cause of his downfall, and they are the ones who helped him in disobedience to Allah.

And so the end of the Samiri was that he isolated himself from his society, and wandered in the wilderness, fleeing from people, so that no one touches him, after the Truth had struck him and its power had confronted him.

How similar this situation is to what happens to a superior, upright youth whom the people of falsehood entice and draw towards their path; and after he has joined their ranks and tasted the pleasure of their falsehood and misguidance, he awakes to the shock of the Truth that brings him to his senses, but only after losing much. Then you see him afterwards fleeing from this companionship and keeping himself far away from even approaching them.

Therefore, among those who choose their religion according to their desires are the worshippers of idols: if worship means that the worshipper obeys his object of worship, then how easy is the worship of idols! For they are gods without obligation, worship without hardship; they restrict no movement for you and do not prevent you from any desire. Otherwise, what reward have the idols prepared for one who worships them? And what punishment have they prepared for one who disbelieves in them?

So it is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted, said to the Samiri: you will be punished by the very society from which you wanted honour, authority, control and remembrance; you will disown them and flee from their neighbourhood, and you will not bear that any of them touch you, for they are the cause of your affliction and the source of your trial, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ (43:67) (az-Zukhruf).

So the friends of falsehood and the companions of evil, who gather in forbidden evening gatherings for disobedience to Allah, should beware of this meeting; but true and sincere friendship belongs to the righteous, who enjoin the truth upon one another and counsel one another to obey Allah.

There is a difference between one who shares the cup with you and one who breaks it and spills it before you taste it; a difference between one who distracts you from prayer and one who urges you to it; a difference between one who makes you happy now with disobedience and one who carries you to the hardship of obedience. So look and reflect.

Then He says: ﴿And indeed for you there is an appointment that you will not be able to break...﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha): that is, what awaits you of the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then scatter it into the sea, a [complete] scattering.﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha).

("ʿAkifan" = remaining constantly in his worship; al-i'tikaf (الاعتكاف) is staying in the mosque and cutting oneself off from the external society.)

The meaning of ﴿Lanuharriqannahu﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha): that is, we will make it like something burned, by grinding it with a file until it becomes crumbs and scattered particles, so that it can be scattered into the air. ﴿Then We will surely scatter it into the sea, a [complete] scattering﴾ (20:97) (Ta-Ha): that is, we will winnow it as farmers do when they winnow grain to separate the husk from it, with an implement called (al-minsaf)(1), resembling a sieve; and they have now replaced these primitive tools with modern mechanical machines that serve the same purpose.

That is because the god of the Samiri was this calf which he made of gold, so burning in fire is not suitable for it; rather, We want for it another process, one that removes it from its origin, so that We leave no trace of it. And this is your god which you worshipped: if it were able, it would defend itself and protect its own soul.

1. Mentioned by Ibn Manzur in (Lisan al-Arab – entry: nasf) where he said: (nasafa al-shay', wa huwa naseef: he sifted it; and an-nasf: cleansing the good from the bad. It is also said of a long sieve: al-minsaf. And al-minsafa: the sieve).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 20, verse 98:

After Allah – glorified be He – had shown the falsehood of what al-Samiri and those who followed him among the people had done, He returned to remind them of the true declaration and the straight path, and that everything they had done was utter nonsense:

﴿Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god; He encompasses all things in knowledge.﴾ (20:98)

When the Truth – blessed and exalted be He – says ﴿There is no god but He…﴾ (20:98), we say it in this same way and bear witness to it. We learned it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who heard it from his Lord and conveyed it to us. It is the testimony to true oneness: a testimony from Allah to His own essence first: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge [also bear witness]…﴾ (3:18).

This is the testimony of the Essence to the Essence before He created any witness to bear it. Then the angels bore witness to it as a witness of direct vision, that there is no god besides Him. Then those of knowledge bore witness to it as a testimony of inference from the created beings they saw, arranged in the most wondrous and marvellous order; and all of this could only arise from a capable God.

This claim is accepted for Allah – exalted be He – because it is a true proposition, testified to by Him for Himself, and testified to by the angels and those of knowledge, and no opponent has arisen to claim it for himself.

Otherwise – God forbid – where is that god from whom Allah took away divinity? Either he does not know, or he knows and does not object; and in both cases he does not deserve to be a god. A claim which is not met with an opponent stands in favour of its claimant until an opponent appears.

It is as if the Truth – glorified be He – said: there is no god but Me, and I am the Creator of the whole universe and its Manager; and no one, even among the disbelievers, has come forward to claim any part of this. We have given an example for this matter – and to Allah belongs the highest similitude: suppose a group of guests and visitors stayed with you, and after they left you found a wallet; you asked about its owner, and no one claimed it until one of them said: it is mine. Thus he is its owner, and he has the better right to it, since no opponent has arisen against him.

Therefore He – exalted be He – says: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say, they would surely have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.﴾ (17:42)

That is, if there were other gods, they would certainly have gone to the Lord of the Throne, either to submit to Him and seek from Him the power to do things, or to call Him to account and contest with Him: how does He claim divinity while they are gods? None of this has happened, and no one has produced proof that he is a god; and a claim for which no proof is established is void.

And the Truth – glorified be He – denies the existence of other gods, saying in another place: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is no god with Him; otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created, and some would have overcome others.﴾ (23:91)

So this one is god of the heavens, that one is god of the earth, this one is god of the jinn, that one is god of mankind, and so on. Thus an advantage in one of them would be a deficiency in another, and power in one would be weakness in another, and this is not fitting for the attributes of divinity.

We note here in His saying – exalted be He – ﴿Your God is only Allah…﴾ (20:98): that the word (ilah) does not mean (Allah); for if (ilah) meant (Allah), the meaning would become: "Only Allah is Allah."

So there is a difference between the two terms: Allah is the proper name for the Necessarily Existent, the Highest Being, whereas (ilah) is the one worshipped and obeyed in what He commands. The meaning, then, is: the one worshipped and obeyed in what He commands is Allah, the Creator of this existence and the Lord of the Highest Being.

Allah – exalted be He – is the one truly worshipped and obeyed, because there are those who are worshipped and obeyed but in falsehood, such as those who worship the sun, the moon, trees and stones and call them gods. If worship means obeying the command and prohibition of the one worshipped, then what did these gods command them, and from what did they forbid them? And what did they prepare for those who worshipped them or who disbelieved in them? So they are worshipped, but in falsehood, because they are gods without a method.

The word ﴿innama⁠﴾ (20:98) (only/indeed) is never used except as a correction of a falsehood, intending to set it right. For example, you say: "Only Zayd came," and you would not say this except to someone who claimed that someone other than Zayd came; it is as if you are saying: "No, so-and-so did not come; only Zayd came."

So the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Your God is only Allah…﴾ (20:98), must have come as a reply to a statement claiming that there is another god. The word ﴿innama⁠﴾ is used only when a matter contrary to what follows is asserted, so it negates the first matter and affirms what follows.

Here He says ﴿Your God is only Allah…﴾ (20:98) because al-Samiri, when he made the calf for them, said: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses…﴾ (20:88). So Allah denied him and corrected the falsehood with the truth: ﴿Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god…﴾ (20:98).

Then the Truth – blessed and exalted be He – added what distinguishes the true God from the false god, saying: ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ (20:98). Because He – glorified be He – is the true God, and this is also a refutation of al-Samiri and of what he took as a god besides Allah. The calf he made has no knowledge; likewise al-Samiri, who commanded people to worship it: had he possessed knowledge, he would have known that his calf would be burned and blown away into the sea by the winds, and he would have known the outcome to which his saying to the people ("no touching") would lead him, and that the punishment of this world would come upon him before the punishment of the Hereafter. Had he known these realities, he would not have undertaken this matter.

The encompassing of Allah's knowledge over all things means: whoever obeys and whoever disobeys. But out of His mercy towards us, He does not call us to account for what He knows of us; rather He teaches us, when we call upon Him, to say: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge…﴾ (40:7). So His mercy precedes our evil deeds and sins, and precedes His punishment and vengeance. In another place He – mighty and majestic – says: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things…﴾ (7:156).

Had we stopped at ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ (20:98) alone, this matter would have exhausted us, for He would requite us for the evil deed and for the good deed; and who could bear this?

Then the Truth – glorified be He – explains the wisdom of the stories in the Qur'an. Stories (qasas) are a kind of history (tarikh), but not history in general. A story is history of a witnessed matter that concerns me and whose knowledge benefits me; otherwise, as history, we would say: "In such-and-such a place there was a man who sold such-and-such, and he used to do this or that."

So a story is a prominent event, with its effect on the one who hears it; through it the admonition is given, and from it the lesson is drawn.

History is the linking of events to their times; when you link any event to its time, you have dated it. If it is a distinct event, we call it a story that is related; if it is a famous story that rises above all stories, we call it a biography (sirah). For this reason the history of the story of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was specifically called sirah, because the story is something distinguished, but the sirah is more distinguished still. The Messenger of Allah was the Seal of the Prophets; therefore we say of his history "sirah" and do not say "qissah", because his reality in life was a going on the path of Allah, the Qur'an was revealed upon it, and his character was the Qur'an.

A story sometimes begins with the event and then the persons revolve around it, or it brings one personality around whom the events revolve. If you wish to write the history of the Urabi Revolution, for example, you place the event first and then mention the persons who revolve around it; if you wish to write the history of the personality of Urabi, you place the personality first and then arrange the events around it.

The stories of the Qur'an differ from the other tales and stories that we hear and tell, which are the composition and invention of human beings. Those are invented stories built upon a knot and its untying: the narrator takes an event and then weaves around it events from his imagination.

Thus they have taken from "qasas" its name but deviated from its meaning. They call this weaving a "qissah", and it is not so, because qissah derives from "qassa al-athar", meaning he followed the trace and its footsteps, not swerving from it nor deviating here or there.

So the story, then, is a precise adherence to events, which does not bear invention or falsification. This is the difference between the stories of the Qur'an, which Allah – the Glorified and Exalted – called ﴿the true narrative﴾ (3:62) and ﴿the best of stories﴾ (12:3), and the stories of men and their compositions.

It is the true story and the best of stories, because it is bound to the truth and does not go beyond it, and it has a lofty purpose, higher than the stories of your world. The aim and essence of the stories of this world, if they succeed, is to protect you from the events of this world; but the protection of the Qur'an's stories is broader, for it protects you in this world and the Hereafter.

If you see repetition in the stories of the Qur'an, know that it serves a purpose and an aim, and that they are various snapshots of different aspects of a single event; when all the snapshots are gathered for you, they give you the complete picture of the event.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 20, verse 99:

Here the Exalted says: ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed before. And We have certainly given you from Ourselves a reminder.﴾ (20:99)

In another place the Exalted said: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart...﴾ (11:120) (Hud)

It is as if his heart, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was in need of being strengthened; for he would encounter all the events of life, and would be exposed to what makes the heads turn grey from its terror. Did not the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, say about the messengers before him: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"...﴾ (2:214) (al-Baqarah).

Did not the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers suffer persecution, beating and siege in the valley (al-Shi'b) without shelter or food, until they ate hides and tree leaves?(1)

These are events and hardships that disturb the human soul when it encounters them, and it necessarily needs the support of heaven in order to remain steadfast in faith. Therefore, the Truth, Blessed and Exalted, relates to His Messenger the stories of those who preceded him in the procession of the messages, to say to him: O Muhammad, you are not an innovation among the messengers; they bore such and such hardships, and you are their chief, so you must bear hardships commensurate with your station. So prepare yourself for this.

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed before...﴾ (20:99): "Thus" means: just as We related to you the story of Musa, Harun, Fir'awn and the Samiri, We relate to you other stories of the news of those messengers who preceded you.

"Anbaa'" (news) is the plural of "naba'", which is the important, great news. So the trivial matter is not called "naba'". Among that is His saying, Exalted, about the Day of Resurrection: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ (78:1-2) (al-Naba'). Rather, one says "khabar" (report) about anything.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And We have certainly given you from Ourselves a reminder.﴾ (20:99)

He emphasised the giving with "from Ourselves" (min ladunna), meaning: from Our presence, i.e., from Us. He did not say, for example, merely "We have given you a reminder." This has a meaning, because all the books that were revealed to the earlier messengers were revealed and narrated in meaning; then their followers formulated them in words of their own. As for the Qur'an, it is the only book that was revealed in both its wording and its meaning. Therefore He said: ﴿from Ourselves﴾ (20:99), that is, directly from Allah to His Messenger.

Whoever contemplates the Messenger's conveying and receiving from his Lord finds that he preserved the wording of the Qur'an, not omitting a single letter from it. For example, in His saying: ﴿Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One"﴾ (112:1) (al-Ikhlas): it would have sufficed in conveying this sentence for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to say: "Allah is One," but he recited the exact text that came to him from his Lord directly.

Do you see that if you said to your son: "Go to your uncle and tell him: My father will visit you tomorrow," would it not suffice for the son to say: "My father will visit you tomorrow"?

Thus, the Qur'an in our hands is itself the speech of Allah revealed to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in which not a single letter has changed, neither by addition nor by subtraction; because it is the text of the miracle, and since it is the text of the miracle, it must remain as Allah said it.

As for the meaning of ﴿reminder﴾ (20:99): "dhikr" has several meanings. "Dhikr" is used and intended to mean the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ (15:9) (al-Hijr).

It is also used and intended to mean fame, nobility and standing in this world, as in His saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder [dhikrukum]﴾ (21:10) (al-Anbiya'), that is, your honour and eminence among people; and He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (43:44) (al-Zukhruf).

Someone may say: how can the Qur'an be a reminder and honour for the Arabs, when it has exposed their inability and revealed their incapacity in eloquence? Can the defeated have fame and honour?

We say: their being defeated by the truth is a testimony that they are strong. The Qur'an rendered the Arabs powerless, and they are a people of eloquence, rhetoric and expression. And the Truth, glorified and exalted, when He challenges, does not challenge the weak; He challenges the strong. It is a source of pride to say: "I defeated such-and-such champion," but what pride is there in saying: "I defeated any ordinary person"?

Likewise, "dhikr" is applied to every book that Allah the Exalted sent down, as He said to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder [ahl al-dhikr] if you do not know﴾ (16:43) (al-Nahl), that is, the people of the reminder before you, namely the people of the Torah and the people of the Gospel.

"Dhikr" is also used and intended to mean doing righteous deeds and the reward from Allah for them, as the Exalted said: ﴿So remember Me; I will remember you...﴾ (2:152) (al-Baqarah), that is: remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with good.

"Dhikr" also comes in the sense of glorification (tasbih) and praise (tahmid), and in the sense of remembrance and taking heed (i'tibar). So it has, therefore, several meanings, determined by the context.

But why did He choose the word "dhikr" and did not say, for example, "kitab" (book)?

They said: because "dhikr" means that you first remember a thing; since it is an important matter that is not forgotten, and it is "dhikr" because it is a source of inspiration, and among the "dhikr" is admonition and reminding; and a thing is only remembered if it has importance. This importance is proportionate to the matter in terms of the duration of its importance and the extent of its importance. Every remembrance of a thing in this world at most gives you the good of this world, whereas the Qur'an is the reminder that gives you the good of both this world and the Hereafter. Therefore it is the most important reminder, which must remain in your mind and never be forgotten.

So the Qur'an is a reminder that is itself remembered first, and a reminder that reminds, and that inspires a reminder encompassing all time, in this world and in the Hereafter.

(1) This was related by al-Bayhaqi in his book "Dala'il al-Nubuwwah" (2/211-214), and its summary is that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered the valley of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib for fear of his uncle Abu Talib, lest the polytheists kill him openly. The polytheists gathered and agreed not to sit with them, trade with them, or enter their houses until they handed over the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to be killed. They wrote a document, covenants and pacts. The Banu Hashim remained for three years, and the affliction and hardship intensified upon them, until the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed his uncle that Allah had told him that the document had been eaten by termites, which left no name belonging to Allah, the Exalted, without eating it, and only injustice, severance and slander remained in it. When Allah corrupted the document of their scheming, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his kin came out and lived and mixed with the people.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, describes this Remembrance, saying:

﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (20:100).

"Turns away" (a‘rada): We know that length is the greatest of distances and breadth is the shortest of distances. Therefore, when Allah, glorified is He, wished to depict for us the vastness of His dominion, He said: ﴿a Garden whose breadth is as the heavens and the earth…﴾ (3:133).

He brought the widest for the narrowest. If its breadth is the heavens and the earth, then what of its length? It must be that it has no end.

Each of us has length and breadth, and breadth is distinguished only by the shoulders, and their view is always from behind, not from the front. Therefore, when a tailor wants to measure a garment for you, he measures it from behind, for a person's breadth is the upper part of the back.

Thus, "he turned away from such-and-such" means: he left it and went far from it, or: he gave it his back and departed from it.

From this is what we say: "Show me the breadth of your shoulders" (i.e., turn your face and leave me). If he is sitting, we say: "Stand up and show me your length" (i.e., stand and show me your height, so that you show me the breadth of your shoulders and depart from me).

Allah, the Exalted, gives us a picture of turning away regarding those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah, saying: ﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard"﴾ (9:35).

Thus you see the punishment arranged according to the arrangement of turning away: first the one who asks is confronted with a frown, he knits his brow and the signs of anger and discomfort appear on him; then he turns his side to him; then he gives him his back and departs from him.

"Wizr" means a heavy load. Would that it were in this world, so you could be rid of it, either by having it removed from you or by escaping it through death. But the burden here is in the Hereafter; therefore it is a heavy burden that does not lift from you and is not escaped by death. It is a load without end and without hope of relief from it; it is heavy and its pain extends. A load may be heavy yet beloved to the soul, like someone carrying something beneficial to himself; but here it is a heavy and hateful load.

Then after that he goes on to qualify the punishment: the one who sins is described as having "carried a burden" (atā wizran).

Sā'a (evil is it): it is evil, that load, on the Day of Resurrection. For a load is not necessarily evil if it is good, but if it is bad, its bearer may carry it in this world and then be rid of it. As for wizr (burden), it is an evil, ugly load, because it lasts in the Abode of Eternity, which has no end.

So when will that be? ﴿On the Day when the Trumpet is blown, and We shall gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:102].

The Day of Resurrection. As for the Trumpet (al-Sur), it is the horn into which the first blast and the second blast will be blown, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and immediately they will be standing, looking on﴾ (az-Zumar: 68).

And the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾ (Ta-Ha: 102):

That is, We will gather them and drive them, zurqan (blue). Zurqah (blueness) is their color, just as you see a person whose face has become congested and whose color has turned blue because of something that befell him. This blueness is the result of the lack of balance and harmony in the body's chemistry from within; it is an inner agitation whose effect appears on the outer skin. So it is as if the terror of the Resurrection and its events produce this blueness in them.

And some(1) interpret ﴿zurqan﴾ (Ta-Ha: 102) to mean: blind. From blueness there arises what results in blindness, and among it are the blue waters that afflict the eye and may cause blindness.

(1) This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. It was mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4418). Al-Qurtubi also mentioned other opinions on the interpretation of (zurqan):
- Thirst, whose intensity has made their eyes turn blue. Said by al-Azhari.
- False hope that is followed by disappointment; it is said: "my eye has turned white from the long waiting for such-and-such."
- The staring of the eye from extreme fear.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 20, verse 103:

That is: in this state in which they are gathered, blue-eyed (zurqan), ﴿they will whisper among themselves, (103)﴾ (Ta-Ha). That is: they speak in low voices, and some of them murmur to others; none of them dares to raise his voice because of the terror of what he sees. The one who is afraid, when he meets from his enemy what he cannot withstand, lowers his voice so that he does not alert the enemy to his place. Or: the matter is so awful that it produces a dread which leaves him no capacity for speech, so he is able to do no more than whisper.

So what is the nature of the whispering (takhafut)? And what do they whisper about?

Some of them say to others in low voices: ﴿"You have not remained but ten (days)," (103)﴾ (Ta-Ha). They say to one another: "We did not remain in the world except ten days." Then the Qur'an clarifies afterwards that this "ten" was their superficial talk, as shown by His words in the next verse: ﴿"The most exemplary of them in conduct will say: 'You have not remained but a day.'" (104)﴾ (Ta-Ha).

Thus the ten shrank to one day, and then the day shrinks to an hour, in His words quoting them: ﴿"And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they did not remain but an hour."﴾ (Ar-Rum, 55). So everything that comes to an end is short.

Therefore: varying statements inclined toward minimization, as if the world, for all the vastness of its lifespan, were nothing but an hour: ﴿"As if they had not remained but an hour of a day."﴾ (Al-Ahqaf, 35).

This minimization of the period of their stay in the world is only due to their bankruptcy and the scarcity of good they sent ahead in it. They were heedless in it, so they left it without fruit; therefore they seek an excuse for themselves in the shortness of the time-span that could have held their deeds, as if they had no time at all for doing good!!

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿We know best what they will say when the best of them in conduct says, "You stayed not but a day."﴾ (20:104).

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, relates to His Messenger (ﷺ) in this world what will be the matter of these criminals in the Hereafter. So when the Resurrection occurs, the scene will come exactly as Allah related it to His Messenger, the very same, because Allah, exalted is He, has encompassed all things in knowledge.

This statement that the Qur'an relates from them is a matter of their own choosing. They heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were able not to say it, but when the Resurrection comes, they will say it word for word, without changing anything of it.

As for His saying ﴿amthaluhum tariqah﴾ (the best of them in conduct) (20:104): it means: the best of them in judgment.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust, scattering (105).﴾

We have spoken about "yas'aluunaka" (they ask you) in His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling... (219)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

The question (su'al) is an interrogative, meaning a request for understanding that needs an answer. A question may come from the ignorant to the knowledgeable, like the student asking his teacher in order to learn the answer, or from the knowledgeable to the ignorant, like the teacher asking his student in order to know the student's standing in knowledge and his acknowledgement of what he knows.

This matter resolved for us a difficulty in which the orientalists were deeply immersed. They say: While the Truth, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So on that Day no one will be asked about his sin, man or jinn (39)﴾ (al-Rahman), He says in another verse: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned (24)﴾ (al-Saffat). The first negates questioning, and the second affirms it. Therefore they accused the Qur'an of contradiction between its verses.

Yet these are to be excused, for they lack the Arabic faculty for understanding the Qur'anic style. The explanation of this difficulty is that a question in the language comes either to learn what you do not know, or to have the one answering confirm what you know, so that it becomes proof against him.

So when the Truth, glorified, says: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned (24)﴾ (al-Saffat), it means a question of confirmation, not a question of inquiry. Thus when He negates the question, He negates the question of knowledge from the side of the speaker, and when He affirms the question, it is the question of confirmation.

The same act is sometimes negated and sometimes affirmed, but the aspect of the negation is separate from the aspect of the affirmation. For example, the Truth, glorified, says to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw... (17)﴾ (al-Anfal).

He negated the act in the first and affirmed it in the second, while the act is one, and the one affirmed and the one negated is one: Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. How do we get out of this difficulty? Did the Messenger throw or did he not throw?

To clarify this matter, we gave the example of a father who sat beside his son so that he could study his lessons. The son began studying, turning the pages of the book. When the father wanted to test how much information he had acquired, he found nothing with him. The son said: "I studied and I did not study." "I studied" means: I performed the act of studying; "I did not study" means: because you have acquired nothing.

So when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, threw, could he have made that throw reach the eyes of the whole army? Hence the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, took a handful of dust and threw it toward the army, but it was the power of Allah that brought this handful of dust and scattered it into the eyes of all the enemies.

Similarly, His saying: ﴿But most people do not know (26)﴾ (al-Jathiyah): He negated knowledge from them, and in another verse: ﴿They know an outward appearance of the life of this world... (7)﴾ (al-Rum): He affirmed for them knowledge.

Returning to His saying: ﴿They ask you about the mountains... (105)﴾ (Ta-Ha). When we surveyed "yas'aluunaka" in the Noble Qur'an, we found its answer preceded by "qul" (say), as in His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people... (219)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

And His saying: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are measures of time for the people and for Hajj... (189)﴾ (al-Baqarah). And so in all the verses, except His saying here: ﴿They ask you about the mountains, so say: My Lord will scatter them as dust, scattering (105)﴾ (Ta-Ha), where the verb "qul" is joined with the fa'. Why?

They said: Because the question in all these verses is a question about something that had already occurred, so the answer came with "qul." For example: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: It is an harm... (222)﴾ (al-Baqarah). As for "They ask you about the mountains... (105)" (Ta-Ha), He said in the answer: "So say: My Lord will scatter them as dust, scattering (105)" (Ta-Ha), because it is an event that has not yet occurred.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, informs His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he will be asked this question, so the fa' here indicates an implied condition, meaning: if they ask you in actuality, then say: such and such.

So the question about the mountains was not at the time of the revelation of the verse, whereas the other questions existed and were asked of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, before the revelation of their verses.

The answer to a question may also come without "qul," as in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, I am near... (186)﴾ (al-Baqarah). Here "qul" or "fa-qul" is not used, because it indicates the directness between Allah, exalted, and His servants, as if the Truth, glorified, makes clear that He is near His servants so near that He dispenses with the answer "qul."

You may wonder: how do all these questions come in the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when the Qur'an is a book of method that brought obligations that may be hard on people, since it binds them to matters that oppose what they desire? It would have been expected that they not ask about matters on which no ruling had been revealed.

We say: these questions of theirs indicate their love for Allah's rulings and obligations. The things that were their customs in the Jahiliyyah they now wished to perform in the manner of Islam, as worship, not merely as a Jahili custom.

Although the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade them from asking, saying: "Leave me as long as I leave you, for those before you were destroyed by their much questioning and their disputing with their prophets" (3).

Nevertheless they asked, and wished that their lives be built upon the method of the Qur'an from Allah, not on it being a habit they were accustomed to in the Jahiliyyah. So these questions are a determination of the matter from the side of the Truth, glorified and exalted.

As for His saying: ﴿So say: My Lord will scatter them as dust, scattering (105)﴾ (Ta-Ha): We have discussed this meaning in His saying: ﴿We will surely burn it and then scatter it into the sea as dust (97)﴾ (Ta-Ha). The intended meaning is: We will crush them and disperse them into the air. He emphasized "nasf" (scattering) by saying: ﴿scattering (97)﴾ (Ta-Ha), to affirm that the mountain will be broken into small particles that the wind scatters.

Some may imagine that the mountains will be leveled and turned into rock masses, as we now blast rocks into large pieces. Therefore he emphasized the scattering, that the mountains will become particles that fly about. Thus He said in another verse: ﴿And the mountains will be like wool, fluffed (5)﴾ (al-Qari'ah), that is: like carded wool.

But why were the mountains mentioned specifically?

They said: Because a person sees himself as a son of change in his own self, and a son of change in what surrounds him of what serves him, whether animal or plant. He sees the animal die or be slaughtered, the plant wilt, then dry and crumble, and man himself dies and ends.

So everything he sees around him manifests change and ending, except the mountains, which he sees as firmly fixed, undergoing no apparent change across the ages.
